full_judgment:
This Rule arises out of the judgment and decree dated 7-3-2004, passed by the Joint District Judge, Fourth Court, Khulna, in Title Appeal No.121 of 1996, affirming those dated 30-5-1996, passed by the Assistant Judge, Batiaghata, Khulna, in Title Suit No.24 of 1996. 

2. Petitioner's predecessor Jotindra Nath Mondal, as plaintiff instituted the suit for declaration of his title over the suit land impleading Gouri Dasi, his mother Samela Mondol, and the Government of Bangladesh as defendant Nos. 1, 2 and 3 respectively. Subsequently the name of defendant No. 2 was struck off. 

3. Plaintiff's case in brief, that his father late Raj Behari Mondal was owner and possessor of the suit land including other lands. He and his deceased brother Avimannya were two sons of Raj Behari Mondal. During lifetime of their father, Avimannya died on 12-8-1958 leaving behind him, father Raj Behari Mondal, their mother Samela Bala Mondal, wife Gouri Dasi, and two daughters. Avimannaya has no son. Raj Behari Mondal died at the age near about 100 years in Salt Lake, Kolkata, wherein they took shelter during the liberation war leaving behind one son the plaintiff, his wife (plaintiff's mother the defendant No.2), and the defendant No.1 Gouri Dasi (widow of deceased Avimannya) According to Daybhaga School of Hindu Law he (plaintiff) is the sole successor in the properties left by his father. Raj Behari Mondal had no other son, grandson, or grand grandson. As such since after their return from India in March 1972 he has been enjoying and possessing the entire property left by his father, and except him nobody has or can claim any right, title and possession over such property. The SA records in respect of the suit land were correctly prepared and finally published in his father's name who had been in enjoyment and possession, and had been paying rent and taxes till the liberation war in 1971. That on 5th Agrahayan 1389 BS he came to know that the defendant No.1 Gouri Dasi Mondal being advised by some evil mongers made an application before the Circle Officer (Revenue), Batiaghata for mutation of 5.95 acres of the suit land in her name, and accordingly 5.95 acres of land was mutated in her name. On 17-1-1983 after obtaining copies of the application made by the defendant No.1 and the order passed thereon from the office of the Circle Officer (Revenue) he became sure about such mutation. The defendant No.1 Gouri Dasi is not entitle to get any Agricultural Land left by Raj Behari Mondal since her husband died during lifetime of his father having no son. As such the order of mutation passed by the Circle Officer (Revenue) is illegal, and not binding upon him. Being asked by him on 20-1-1983 the defendant No.1 replied that the Circle Officer (Revenue) said her that, even after death of her husband during his father's lifetime she will get 50% of the property left her father-in-law. She threatened him that in case of objection in taking possession of such property she will sale the same to any mighty person. The defendants have no right, title and possession over the suit land since they are not entitle to get the same. He is the only successor in the suit land left by his father. The suit land is Agricultural Land and the defendants cannot claim any right, title possession over the same. Hence, to avoid future complications, instituted the suit. 

4. The defendant No.1 Gouri Dasi contested the suit by filing written statement and subsequent additional written statements. She denied the material allegations and stated, that the suit is not maintainable in its present form and there is no cause of action to institute the suit; that Raj Behari Mondal died in 1971 AD leaving the plaintiff, the defendant No.1 and two granddaughters named Kali Dasi and Gita Rani by his deceased son; that she inherits the suit land being stepping in the shoes of her deceased husband as per the provision of law provides in section 3 of the Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937; that as per that law she got half of the properties left by Raj Behari Mondal, and, as such, mutated the suit land in her name; that she sold a part of the same to different persons and handed over possession and has been enjoying and possessing the rest; that the plaintiff also transferred some land from his 50% share succeeded from his father to different persons by executing different deeds, but without impleading those purchasers instituted the suit, that amongst her two daughters one named Gita Rani has 3 (three) son's and, as such, she will succeed the suit property; that her daughters Kali Dasi, Gita Rani, and sons of Gita Rani were also not impleaded as defendants, as such the suit also suffers from defect of parties. 

5. After hearing the parties the Assistant Judge, Batiaghata, Khulna, by the judgment and decree dated 30-5-1996 dismissed the suit finding that the suit is not maintainable in its present form without prayer for any consequential relief and for nonpayment of Advolarum Court fees, though found that the defendant No.1 Gouri Dasi is not entitle to get the Agricultural Land left by her father-in-law. 6. Title Appeal No.121 of 1996, preferred against the said judgment and decree by the plaintiff was dismissed by the impugned judgment and decree dated 7-3-2004, passed by the Joint District Judge, Fourth Court, Khulna, finding with others that the defendant No.1 Gouri Dasi is entitle to inherit the suit land left by her father-in-law Raj Behari Mondal. 

7. Hence, the petitioners preferred this revision and obtained the Rule. 

8. Mr MA Jabber, learned Advocate, appearing for the petitioners submits that the trial Court illegally dismissed the suit finding as not maintainable in its present form, though rightly found that the defendant No.1 Gouri Dasi will not be entitled to get any share in the Agricultural Land left by her father-in-law Raj Behari Mondal as widow of his predeceased son Avimannya, but the Appellate Court committed illegality in dismissing the appeal reversing such finding of the trial Court regarding Agricultural Land, though the defendant No.1 did not prefer any appeal or cross objection against such finding. 

9. He further submits, that any widow of a predeceased son of a person like Raj Behari Mondal will not inherit the Agricultural Land left by him or his son, rather she will only inherit the Homestead for her life time. 

10. Mr Jabber by mentioning a decision submits further that the question whether any such lady will inherit any such Agricultural Land was raised in a case, and for dispelling out such dispute a Reference was made by the then British India Government to the Federal Court. In that case the Federal Court by its decision as it reported in 45 CWN Page-81 hold that as per the provision of law provides in "The Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937" no widow of any predeceased son will inherit any Agricultural Land, and by that decision the said Act had been nullified and it has got no effect in our country or in present India. As such, the Appellate Court committed illegality in allowing the defendant Gouri Dasi to inherit the Agricultural Land left by her father-in-law Raj Behari Mondal. 

11. In support of his contention Mr Jabbar cited the decisions reported in AIR 1941 Federal Court 72, 22 DLR 359 and 36 DLR 155. 

12. In reply, Mr Syed Nafiul Islam, learned Advocate, appearing for the defendant/ respondent/opposite party No.1 Gouri Dasi submits that the Appellate Court did not commit any illegality in deciding the question whether the defendant/respondent Gouri Dasi will inherit the suit land in absence of any appeal or cross objection by her, and rightly found that she is entitle to inherit the suit land. He further submits, that in the original Act the word "Agricultural Land" was not included, but subsequently finding necessity, the said Act was amended, and further new acts were made in different states/provinces of India and Pakistan extending such rights even to Agricultural Land. 

13. Mr Islam placed the "The Hindu Women's Right to Property (Extension to Agricultural Land) Act 1943, (Assam Act No. XIII of 1943), and submits that by the said Act the rights allowed under "The Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937, was extended in the then Sylhet District even to the Agricultural Land. 

14. However, he did not place any such Act made in any other state/province of the then India or Pakistan. 

15. As per Mr Islam, the Bangladesh have been following The Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937. As per the said Act, property includes all properties, not any particular kind of property like Agricultural or Non Agricultural Land, or Homestead etc. He placed the said Act i.e. "The Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937" (Act No. XVIII of 1937) as it was applicable in Pakistan, which was adopted in Bangladesh after its emergence with an amendment made by the Bangladesh Laws (revision and declaration) Act, 1973 (Act No. VIII of 1973) substituting the word "Pakistan" by the word "Bangladesh" in its section 1(2). By placing the said Act as applicable in Bangladesh he submits that, as per Section 3 of the said Act, defendant Gouri Dasi will inherit 50% of all the properties left by her father-in-law. 

16. After hearing the learned Advocates of both the parties I feel it better to hear any other learned Advocate as Amicus Curie, and directed Mr Uzzal Bhowmick, to assist the court. Accordingly, Mr Uzzal Bhowmick, appeared as Amicus Curie and submits, that in the original Act made on 14th April 1937 (Act XVIII of 1937) the Agricultural Land was not included and, as such, the reference as reported in 45 CWN was made by the then British India Government to the Federal Court, and in that decision the question of Agricultural Land was decided in negative. That the administration of Agricultural Land had not been regulating by the central government of India, rather it was the business of the provincial/state governments. As such, the central Governments of India amended the said Act inserting the words "any property", after partition, the Pakistan has been following the same. Thereafter in some states/ provinces of India and Pakistan like Assam, Sindh, Hyderabad, North-West Frontier Province, Punjab by making new acts or ordinances extended such rights even to the "Agricultural Land", after subsequent amendments of the Act No. XVIII of 1937, the said decision of the Federal Court as cited by Mr MA Jabber has got no manner of application. 

17. By mentioning Section 3 of the said Act as it adopted in Bangladesh after its emergence Mr Bhowmick submits that the defendant Gouri Dasi is entitle to inherit 50% of all properties left by her father-in-law Raj Behari Mondal as widow of his predeceased son Avimannya. He further submits that the Appellant Court has got the authority to reverse any illegal finding of the trial Court even in absence of any appeal or cross objection preferred by the defendant/respondent. 

18. In support of his contention Mr Bhowmick cited the decisions in the cases of, Sheik Md Siddique vs Hari Lal Nath and others reported in 22 DLR 359, Rai Kishori Saha vs Md Motalehb Ali and others reported in 1983 BLD, Page-1 and also in 34 DLR 178, an unreported judgment of the Supreme Court of India dated 18-11-1998 passed in the appeal of VAIJANATH and others vs GURAMMA and another, arises out of a judgment passed by the Hyderabad High Court deciding same question about Agricultural Land, and regarding the question about absence of any appeal or cross objection by the defendant/respondent he cited the decision in the case of Hazrat Ali and others vs Yakub Ali Khan and others, reported in 1983 BLD (AD) Page 62. 

19. After hearing the learned Advocates, I have gone through the judgments of the courts below and other materials on record, the decisions cited by learned Advocates and mentioned in the judgment of the trial court, and the concern law mentioned above. 

20. On perusal of the judgments of the Courts below it appears, that the trial Court dismissed the suit on the question of maintainability, but decided the question about defendant's right in Agricultural land left by her father-in-law in negative. As per the trial Court the defendant Gouri Dasi will not be entitled to inherit any Agricultural Land left by her father-in-law in its judgment the trial Court mentioned the decisions reported in 22 DLR 359, 34 DI ,R 179, 36 DLR 155, and the aforesaid decision reported in 45 CWN.

21. The Appellate Court reversed such finding of the trial Court, and as per the appellate Court the defendant Gouri Dasi will inherit the suit land left by her father-in-law as widow of his predeceased son Avimannya. 

22. On perusal of the materials on record it appears that Raj Behari Mondal, the admitted owner of the suit land was father of two sons named Jotindra Nath Mondal (plaintiff) and Avimannya. Admittedly Avimannya died during his life time leaving behind his widow the defendant Gouri Dasi and two daughters named Gita Rani and Kali Dasi. It is also apparent that Gita Rani is mother of three sons. Admittedly after death of Avimannaya his widow defendant Gouri Dasi had been residing with her father-in-law, and after his death has been residing in the Homestead left by him. The plaintiff did not make any statement how Gouri Dasi has been earning her livelihood. For a human being, only the Homestead is not enough to survive, rather he/she has other necessity like food, clothes, medicine, treatment etc, and to bear cost of those he/she requires income from any source, which may be the Agricultural Land. 

23. As per the plaintiff, the defendant Gouri Dasi can inherit the Homestead left by Raj Behari Mondal, but not the disputed Agricultural Land. The defendant Gouri Dasi has been claiming that being stepping in the shoes of her deceased husband she will inherit 50% of all properties left by her father-in-law including the disputed Agricultural Land. 

24. To decide the question whether the defendant Gouri Dasi is entitle to inherit the Agricultural Land as she claims the concern law required to followed is "The Hindu Women's Right to Property Act, 1937 (Act No. XVIII of 1937)" which was subsequently amended by "The Hindu Women's Rights to Property (Amendment) Act, 1938, (Act No. II of 1938)". The said Act was enacted on 14th April, 1937 in the then British India. The statements of object and reason to enact such law had been published in the Gazette of India, 1935, Part V, Page-131. The said Act as applicable in the then British India is as follows:- 
Central Government Act 
The Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937
(Act No. XVIII of 1937)
14th April 1937
An Act to amend the Hindu Law governing Hindu Women's Rights to property. 
WHEREAS it is expedient to amend the Hindu Law to give better rights to women in respect of property; It is hereby enacted as follows:— 
1. Short title and extent.—(1) This Act may be called the Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937. 
(2). It extends to all the provinces and the capital of the Federation. 
2. Application.—Notwithstanding any rule of Hindu Law or custom to the contrary, the provisions of section 3 shall apply where a Hindu dies intestate leaving a widow. 
3. Devolution of property— (1) When a Hindu governed by the Dayabhaga School of Hindu Law dies intestate leaving any property, and when a Hindu governed by any other school of Hindu Law or by customary law dies intestate leaving separate property, his widow, or if there is more than one widow, all his widows together, shall, subject to the provisions of sub-section (3), be entitled in respect of property in respect of which he dies intestate to the same share as a son. 
Provided that the widow of a predeceased son shall inherit in like manner as a son if there is no son surviving of such predeceased son, and shall inherit in like manner as a son's son if there is surviving a son or son's son of such predeceased son: 
Provided further that the same provision shall apply mutatis mutandis to the widow of a predeceased son of a predeceased son. 
(2) When a Hindu governed by any school of Hindu Law other than the Dayabhaga School or by customary law dies intestate having at the time of his death an interest in a Hindu joint family property, his widow shall, subject to the provisions of sub-section (3), have in the property the same interest as he himself had. 
(3) Any interest devolving on a Hindu widow under the provisions of this section shall be the limited interest known as a Hindu woman's estate, provided however that she shall have the same right of claiming partition as a male owner. 
(4) The provisions of this section shall not apply to an estate which by a customary or other rule of succession or by the terms of the grant applicable thereto descends to a single heir or to any property to which the Succession Act, 1925 applies. 
4. Nothing in this Act shall apply to the property of any Hindu dying intestate before the commencement of this Act. 
5. For the purposes of this Act, a person shall be deemed to die intestate in respect of all property of which he has not made a testamentary disposition which is capable of taking effect. 

25. After partition of India, the said Act No. XVIII of 1937 made by the then central Government of India was adopted in Pakistan with an amendment in its section 1(2) made by the Central Laws (Statute Reform) Ordinance, 1960 (Ordinance No.XXI of 1960). By amending the said section the area to extent was changed as the "whole of Pakistan". Bangladesh was a part of Pakistan, and after its emergence, the said Act as applicable in Pakistan has been adopted by amending its section 1(2) only substituting the word "Pakistan" by the word "Bangladesh". Such amendment and adoption has been made by the Bangladesh Laws (Revision and Declaration) Act 1973, (Act No. VIII of 1973). 

26. It is the history that before partition of India, the then Sylhet district (composed of present Sylhet avision of Bangladesh and some other area of India like Karimganj) was included in its Assam province after division of the then Bengal. Such rights to the Hindu Women of the then Sylhet District was extended even up to the Agricultural Land by enacting the Assam Act No. XIII of 1943, which is as follows:- 
The Hindu Women's Rights to Property (Extension to Agricultural Land) Act, 1943. 
(Assam Act No. XIII of 1943). 
An Act to extend the operation of the Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937 and the Hindu Women's Rights to Property (Amendment) Act, 1938, to Agricultural Land in the District of Sylhet. 
WHEREAS the Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937, and the Hindu Women's Rights to Property (Amendment) Act, 1938, purport to give better rights to women in respect of property in general; 
WHEREAS transactions have already taken place in the province on the basis that women had acquired better rights under the said acts in respect of Agricultural Land as well as other kinds of property; 
WHEREAS it has now been established that the said acts do not operate to give them better rights in respect of Agricultural Land; 
WHEREAS in order to validate those transactions as well as to give women in future those better rights and for other purposes, it is expedient to extend the operation of the said acts to Agricultural Land with retrospective effect, but with certain savings; 
It is hereby enacted as follows:- 
(1) Short title and extent.-This Act may be called the Hindu Women's Rights to 
Property (Extension to Agricultural Land) Act, 1943. 
 (2) It extends to the whole of the District of Sylhet. 
(3) Commencement-It shall come into force at once. 
2. The term "property" in the Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937, and the Hindu Women's Rights to Property (Amendment) Act, 1938, shall include, and shall be deemed always to have included, Agricultural Land. 
Provided that where any person who, but for this Act, would have been entitled to any property has been in possession or has made a transfer thereof, his possession till the commencement of this Act shall be deemed to be as lawful, and the transfer made by him shall be deemed to be as valid, as if this Act had not been passed. 

27. The said Act is till in force in the Sylhet Division of Bangladesh since it has not yet been repealed. 

28. On reading preamble of the said Assam Act No. XIII of 1943, it appears that the Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937 and the Hindu Women's Rights to Property (Amendment) Act, 1938 purport to give better rights to women in respect of Property in General. And on the basis of that women had acquired better rights under those acts in respect of Agricultural Land as well as other kinds of property transactions had already taken place in the province, but the acts do not operate to give them better rights in respect of Agricultural Land, as such it was expedient to extend the operation of the said acts to Agricultural Land with retrospective effect in order to validate those transaction, as well as to give women in future those better rights and for other purposes. As per section 2 of the said Act the term "property" in the Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937 and the Hindu Women's Rights to Property (Amendment) Act, 1938, shall include , shall be deemed always to have been included , Agricultural Land. 

29. Similar laws had also been made extending such rights in other provinces. For example, in North-West Frontier Province by the "North West Frontier Province Hindu Women's Rights to Property (Extension to Agricultural land) Act, 1942 (Governor's Act No. VI of 1942), in Sindh, by The Hindu Women's Right to Property (extension to Agricultural Land) Act, 1942 (Act No. IX of 1942), such rights has been extended to Agricultural Land. 

30. Reading preamble of the Assam Act No. XIII of 1943 and such acts in other provinces of India extending Hindu Women's Rights to Agricultural Land as mentioned above, and the said acts of 1937 and 1938, it appears that the purpose of making such acts are nothing but to amend the Hindu Law giving right to Hindu Women's to all properties. 

31. The preamble of said Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937 (Act No. XVIII of 1937) as it applicable in the then India, Pakistan and Bangladesh, reveals that, the objects and purpose of making such law was to amend the Hindu Law governing Hindu Women's Rights to Property at the relevant time. Subsequently to ensure better rights to women such acts were enacted to extend such rights to "property in general" including the Agricultural Land. 

32. Section 2 of the Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937 (Act No. XVIII of 1937) provides that, notwithstanding any rule of Hindu Law or custom to the contrary, the provisions of section 3 of the said Act shall apply where a Hindu "dies intestate" leaving a widow. Section 5 of the said Act provides the meaning of the expression "die intestate". As per said section, for the purpose of the said Act, a person shall be deemed to "die intestate" in respect of property of which he has not made a testamentary disposition which is capable of taking effect. 

33. Section 3(1) of the said Act provides that, "When a Hindu governed by the Dayabhaga School of Hindu Law dies intestate leaving any property, and when a Hindu governed by any other school of Hindu Law or by customary law dies intestate leaving separate property, his widow, or if there is more than one widow, all his widows together, shall, subject to the provisions of sub-section (3), be entitled in respect of property in respect of which he dies intestate to the same share as a son. 

34. Provided that the widow of a pre-deceased son shall inherit in like manner as a son if there is no son surviving of such predeceased son, and shall inherit in like manner as a son's son if there is surviving a son or son's son of such predeceased son: 
Provided further that the same provision shall apply mutatis mutandis to the widow of a predeceased son of a predeceased son. 

35. As per section 3 of the said Act No. XVIII of 1937 a Hindu Widow is entitle to inherit the property left by her deceased husband, and even widow of a predeceased son of the deceased is also entitle to inherit the property left by him as his son. 

36. Reading the said Act of 1937 as applicable in Bangladesh, I do not find specification of any particular property in it. The word "property" means all properties which may be movable or immovable, Homestead, Agricultural Land, any other properties in cash or in kind. There is no scope to distinguish between the Agricultural Land and Homestead since both such properties and others are necessary for survival of a widow. I find no reason to inherit the Homestead only by the defendant Gouri Dasi the admitted widow of Avimannya, a predeceased son of Raj Behari Mondal, and to deprive her from the disputed Agricultural Land. After death her father-in-law Gouri Dasi admittedly has been residing in the Homestead left by him, and apparently, for her livelihood she is dependent upon the Agricultural Land left by him. 

37. In the instant case the defendant Gouri Dasi is admittedly governed by Dayabhaga school of Hindu law, and no testament was made by her father-in-law. So as per the provisions of section 3(1) of the Act XVIII of 1937 she will inherit 50% of all properties left by her father-in-law as like his predeceased son. 

38. It is also admitted that Avimannya died leaving behind two daughters names Kali Dasi and Gita Rani who has three male issue (sons). So I hold the view that, on death of Raj Behari Mondal, widow of his predeceased son Avimannya will inherit the property left by him, and thereafter the grandsons of Avimannya by his admitted daughter Gita Rani will succeed the same. 

39. On perusal of decisions cited above I find that, regarding the question of right of Gouri Dasi the decision in the case of Rai Krishna vs Md Matleb AU Pramanik and others reported in 3 BLD and also in 34 DLR 178 and the abovementioned unreported judgment of the Supreme Court of India are relevant, and the others cited by the learned Advocates and mentioned in the trial court's judgment have no manner of application in the instant case. 

40. In the case of Rai Krishna vs Md Matleb Ali Pramanik and others reported in 3 BLD and also in 34 DLR 178 it was held that the Hindu widow during her life time is a complete owner and co-sharer of any property or holding in question has the right to claim partition and pre-emption. 

41. In the aforesaid unreported decision of the Supreme court of India their lordships found that the language of the Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937 is wide enough to cover Agricultural Land also, in the entire Hindu Women's Right to Property Act, 1937, there is nothing which would indicate that the Act does not apply to Agricultural Land. The word "property" is a general term which covers all kinds of property, including Agricultural Land. A restricted interpretation was given to the original Hindu Women's Right to Property Act, 1937 enacted by the then Central Legislature, entirely because of the legislative entries in the Government of India Act, 1935, which excluded the legislative competence of the Central Legislature over Agricultural Lands. 

42 On perusal of the finding of the trial Court and the decisions mentioned in its judgment it appears to me that the learned Judge of the trial Court was confused about the decisions mentioned, and arrived into wrong decision about the right of defendant Gouri Dasi without perusal of the law in force or being failure to understand the provisions of the law in its proper aspect. 

43. After perusal of the law of the land as discussed above and the decisions cited above, I find that the finding of the appellate Court regarding the right of Gouri Dasi in the disputed suit land is correct and I do not find any illegality about the question of inheritance as decided by the Appellate Court. 

44. Regarding the question of cross objection, I hold the view that the appellate court can decide any question of law and fact even in absence of any cross objection or appeal by the defendant/respondent as it made in the instant case. My such view got support from the decision reported in 1983 BLD (AD) 62 as mentioned above. 

45. Accordingly, I find that by the impugned judgment no failure of justice has been caused. 

Hence, the Rule is hereby discharged. However, there is no order as to costs. 

Send down the lower Court's records immediately. 

End.

lawyer:
Md Ismail Miah, Advocate with Md Solaiman Munshi, Advocate—For the Appellant.

Md Hashmat Ullah Sheikh, Advocate with Gazi Md Neamat Hossain, Advocate with Sheikh Shah Imran, Advocate—For the Respondent No. 3.
parties:
Mirza International Ltd. -------- Appellant
VS
Registrar, Department of Patents, Designs and Trade Mark, Dhaka and others   ------- Respondents
full_judgment:
SM Maniruzzaman, J: The instant trade mark appeal has been preferred against the decision and order dated 10-1-2013 passed by the respondent No. 1, Registrar, Patents, Designs and Trade Mark, (in short, the Registrar) Dhaka rejecting Opposition Case No. 2635 of 2010 and allowing Trade Mark Application being No. 92081 in Class-25 filed by the respondent No. 3. 

2. Facts, relevant for disposal of the appeal, in short, are that the opponent appellant M/s Mirza International Ltd. is a private limited company duly incorporated under the existing Companies Act in India and is engaged in the business of manufacturing, merchanting and exporting all kinds of footwears, readymade garments and clothing, leather goods, leather garments, leather belt, headgears and other various goods. The appellant is the registered proprietor of trade mark "RED TAPE" in India in various classes. However, the trade mark "RED TAPE" of the appellant has been registered and used in various countries of the world i.e. in Australia, Canada, European Union, Great Britain, Hongkong, New Zealand, Singapore, United Arab Emirates and USA as a well known and famous trade mark. 

3. Therefore, in order to protect the right, title and interest of the trade mark "RED TAPE", the opponent appellant applied for registration trade mark "RED TAPE" in Bangladesh before the respondent No.1, Registrar, Department of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks, Dhaka being Registration No. 137614 in Class-25 dated 14-11-2010. Said application, however, is still pending for consideration of the concerned authority. During pendency of the said application, the appellant came to know that the exactly similar trade mark "RED TAPE" has been advertised in the Trade Marks Journal No. 251 at Page- 4294 in Bangladesh under the Trade Mark Application No. 92081 in Class-25 in the name of respondent No. 3, Sohel Rana, sole proprietor of THAI TEX of BB Road, Ukil Para, Narayangong, Bangladesh. However, the present appellant is the registered proprietor of the trade mark "RED TAPE" in India in Class-25 for the same goods and same description of the goods, which is a gross violation of Article 6b6 of the Paris Convention and Article 16(2) & (3) of the TRIPS Agreement relating to the protection of well known trade mark. 

4. Being aggrieved by the said advertisement published in the Trade Mark Journal, the appellant as opponent filed Opposition Case No. 2635 of 2010 before the respondent No. 1, Registrar.

5. The respondent No. 3 contested the opposition case by filing counter statement (TM-6) and also submitted evidences in support of his claim contending inter alia that the respondent No. 3 is the sole proprietor of THAI TEX and adopted trade mark with unique design and get-up used on his products under the word "red tape" in the year, 2000. Since then, said mark is being used continuously and extensively with great fame and name without any objection from any quarter in Bangladesh. He has adopted the said trade mark "red tape" for special type of products i.e. clothing, footwear, headgear and all others goods included in Class-25. Accordingly, he applied for registration before the 'respondent No. 1, Registrar being Application No. 92081 in Class-25 dated 14-6-2005 but the opponent appellant filed the opposition case against the advertisement of the trade mark "red tape" published in the Trade Mark journal due to the business jealously and to harass him. The appellant has never used any class of goods under the trade mark "RED TAPE" or similar or identical in the local market in Bangladesh. 

6. The respondent No. 1, Registrar upon hearing the contending parties, considering the evidences on record and submissions so advanced by both the parties rejected the opposition case and allowed the Trade Mark Application of the respondent No. 3 being No. 92081 in Class-25 vide order and decision dated 10-1-2013. 

7. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid order and decision dated 10-1-2013 passed by the respondent No. 1, Registrar, the appellant preferred the instant trade mark appeal under section 100 of the Trade Mark Act, 2009 (in short, the Act, 2009). 

8. Mr Md Ismail Miah, the learned Advocate appearing with Mr Md Solaiman Munshi, the learned Advocate for the appellant submits that the respondent No.1, Registrar failed to appreciate that the appellant's trade mark "RED TAPE" being registered in India would be protected under the provision of Article 61'6 of the Paris Convention and Articles 16(2) & (3) of the TRIPS Agreement within the meaning of "well known trade mark" but the Registrar without considering the such legal position rejected the opposition case of the appellant and allowed the registration of the trade mark "red tape" in favour of the respondent No. 3; hence, the impugned order and decision passed by the respondent No. 1 is liable to be set-aside. He next submits that the Registrar ought to have considered the fact that the trade mark of the appellant is a well known trade mark in the world which was registered in other countries of the world under the International Treaties and Bangladesh is one of the signatory member country of the said convention. The Registrar without considering the such contention rejected the appellant's Opposition Case No. 2635 of 2010 and allowed the Trade Mark Application being No. 92081 in Class-25 of the respondent No. 3. He further submits that the appellant has a prima-facie case and has proved its case by filing materials of evidence in support of its case including registration certificates of different countries of the world in respect of trade mark "RED TAPE" but the Registrar without considering the said evidences on record rejected the appellant's opposition case holding inter alia;- “পর্যালোচনা ও উপস্থাপিত তথ্য প্রমাণাদি�� ভিত্তিতে ট্রাইব্যুনালের নিকট প্রমাণিত হয়েছে যে, অপোনেন্টের "RED TAPE" মার্ক বাংলাদেশের বাজারে নেই বা অপরিচিত এবং দরখাস্তকারীর মার্কটি বাংলাদেশের বাজারে সুপরিচিত ও দরখাস্তকারীর প্রতিষ্ঠানের মার্ক বলে পরিচিতি লাভ করেছে।” Such findings of the Registrar is wrong and inconsistent with the provision of law; as such, the impugned order and decision is liable to be set-aside. He further goes to submit that the appellant is a registered proprietor of trade mark "RED TAPE" in India under the Madrid Protocol (WIPO) being Registration No. 688723 in Classes-18, 24, 25 and 28 and the reputation and goodwill of the said mark is a well known trade mark in the world and also spills over to Bangladesh by virtue of advertisement through internet and that the goods under the trade mark "RED TAPE" are exported into Bangladesh. In that view, the trade mark of the appellant is being used in Bangladesh prior to the respondent's trade mark. Furthermore, the appellant is exclusive proprietor of the trade mark "RED TAPE" but the Registrar without considering such point of law rejected the appellant's opposition case and allowed the trade mark application of the respondent No. 3. 

9. In support of the aforesaid arguments, the learned Advocate for the appellant has relied on the decision in the case of Sunil Kumar Das vs Canon Kabushiki Kaisha and another reported in 2005 BLD (AD) 146 = 10 BLC (AD) 92 and 57 DLR (HC) 93. 

10. Conversely, Mr Md Hashmat Ullah Sheikh, the learned Advocate appearing with Mr Gazi Md Neamat Hossain, the learned Advocate for the respondent No. 3 by drawing attention to the impugned order and decision submits that the respondent No. 1, Registrar after hearing the contending parties, considering the evidences on record and existing provisions of law rejected Opposition Case No. 2635 of 2010 and allowed the application for registration of the respondent's trade mark "red tape"; as such, there is no illegality in the impugned order and decision. He next submits that the appellant did not produce any evidence before the Registrar to the effect that any product under the trade mark "RED TAPE" is available in the local market in Bangladesh and that said trade mark is being used in Bangladesh market. But the respondent's trade mark "red tape" has been using in the local market in Bangladesh since 2000 after manufacturing and supplying the items of hosiery, garments and others goods including goods in Class-25. The Registrar considering the said facts rightly rejected the opposition case of the appellant. He further submits that the present respondent filed application for registration of the trade mark "red tape" being Trade Mark Application No. 92081 in Class-25 dated 14-6-2005 being used since 1999 and on the other hand, the appellant has filed application for registration of the trade mark "RED TAPE" being Application No. 137614 in Class-25 dated 14-11-2010. In view of the above fact, it is proved that the respondent's trade mark application is the prior application to the appellant's application and considering the said legal aspect, the Registrar rightly rejected opposition case of the appellant. He also goes to submit that the trade mark "REP TAPE" of the appellant is not a well known mark in Bangladesh and it is not used in Bangladesh and, as such, Article 6b's of the Paris Convention is not applicable to the appellant's case; hence, the appellant's trade mark "RED TAPE" cannot be treated as a well-known mark in Bangladesh under the Trade Mark Act, 2009. Lastly, he argues that the respondent's trade mark "red tape" is the more senior trade mark of the appellant's trade mark in Bangladesh and the same is being used in the local market in Bangladesh since 1999. Moreover, the respondent filed application for registration of the trade mark "red tape" being Application No. 92081 in Class-25 on 14-6-2005; on the other hand, the appellant filed application for registration of trade mark "RED TAPE" being Application No. 137617 in Class-25 on 14-11-2010. Considering the said legal aspect the respondent No. 1, Registrar rightly rejected the opposition case of the appellant vide the impugned order and decision. 

11. In support of the aforesaid arguments, the learned Advocate for the respondent has relied on the decisions of the case of Abdul Motaleb vs Haji Aftab Miah, reported in 16 BL7' (HCD) 138, Nabisco Biscuit and Bread Factory Limited, Dhaka vs Baby Food Products Limited, Dhaka reported in 2008 BLD (HCD) 304, SM Taufiq vs National Biscuit Co., New York, reported in PLD 1962 ( WP) Karachi 355 and Anwar Hossain (Md), proprietor of M/s Pride Knit Wear Ltd. vs Registrar, Patents, Designs and Trade Mark, Dhaka and another 25 BLC 264, Samah Razor Blades Industries Ltd. vs Supermax International Pvt. Ltd and another 51 DLR 237 and in the case of Bally Schutrabriken Ag, Swizerland vs Hosnara Begum reported in 52 DLR 546. 

12. We have heard the learned Advocate for the appellant, the learned Advocate for the respondent No. 3, have perused the impugned order and decision, memo of appeal and the relevant materials on record so appended thereto. 

13. In the instant appeal admittedly the opponent appellant applied for registration of the trade mark "RED TAPE" before the respondent No. 1, Registrar.on 14-11-2010 being Trade Mark Application No. 137614 in Class-25 claiming that the appellant's trade mark "RED TAPE" was registered in India since, 1997. Subsequently, said trade mark was registered in various countries of the world. Conversely, the respondent No. 3, Sohel Rana, one sole proprietor of M/s THAI TEX applied for registration of trade mark "red tape" being Trade Mark Application No. 92081 in Class-25 dated 14-6-2005 claiming that the trade mark "red tape" is being used in Bangladesh since, 1999. In view of the said undisputed admitted position of fact that the respondent No. 3 filed application for registration trade mark before the Registrar in Bangladesh prior to the appellant's application. Considering the said context, the respondent No.1, Registrar passed the impugned order and decision holding inter alia; 
“অপর দিকে দরখাস্তকারীর “red tape” মার্কটি বাংলাদেশের বাজারে ব্যাপক পরিচিতি লাভ করেছে এবং আরো দেখা যায় বে, দরখাস্তকারীর মার্ক এর দরখাস্ত নম্বর ৯২০৮১, শ্রেণী-২৫ অথচ অপোনেন্টের দরখাস্ত নম্বর ১৩৭৬১৪, শ্রেণী-২৫। সুতরাং দরখাস্তের দিক হতে ও অপোনেন্টের দরখাস্ত অনেক অনেক পরের । অর্থাৎ দরখাস্তকারীর দরখাস্ত Prior FAIRE সে কারণে Trademarks Act, 2009 অনুযায়ী অগ্রাধিকার (Prior user).

সিদ্ধান্ত ও কারণঃ পর্যালোচনা ও উপস্থাপিত তথ্য প্রমাণাদির ভিত্তিতে ট্রাইব্যুনালের নিকট প্রমাণিত হয়েছে যে, অপোনেন্টের “RED TAPE” মার্ক বাংলাদেশের বাজারে নেই বা অপরিচিত এবং দরখাস্তকারীর মার্কটি বাংলাদেশের বাজারে সুপরিচিত ও দরখাস্তকারীর প্রতিষ্ঠানের মার্ক বলে পরিচিত লাভ করেছে। সুতরাং অপোজিশন মামলা নং ২৬৩৫/২০১০ না-মঞ্জুর যোগ্য।”

14. However, the moot contention of the appellant in the instant appeal is that the respondent No. 1, the Registrar without considering the provision of Articles 6 and 6L of the Paris Convention passed the impugned order and decision, as because, the appellant's trade mark "RED TAPE" was registered in India as well as in other countries of the world prior to the date of filing application for registration by the respondent No. 3 before the respondent No. 1, Registrar in Bangladesh. Moreover, the trade mark "RED TAPE" is a well known trade mark in the world. 

15. In order to appreciate the said argument of the appellant let us first have a look at the relevant provision of Articles 6 and of the Paris Convention, which are quoted below for ready reference; 
"Article-6 
"[Marks: Conditions of Registration; Independence of Protection of Same Mark in Different Countries] 
(1) The conditions for the filing and registration of trade marks shall be determined in each country of the Union by its domestic legislation. 
(2) However, an application for the registration of a mark filed by a national of a country of the Union in any country of the Union may not be refused, nor may a registration be invalidated, on the ground that filing, registration, or renewal, has not been effected in the country of origin. 
(3) A mark duly registered in a country of the Union shall be regarded as independent of marks registered in the other countries of the Union, including the country of origin." 
"Article 6'' 
[Marks: Well-Known marks]
(1) The countries of the Union undertake, ex-officio if their legislation so permits, or at the request of an interested party, to refuse or to cancel the registration, and to prohibit the use, of a trademark which constitutes a reproduction, an imitation, or a translation, liable to create confusion, of a mark considered by the competent authority of the country of registration or use to be well known in that country as being already the mark of a person entitled to the benefits of this convention and used for identical or similar goods. These provisions shall also apply when the essential part of the mark constitutes a reproduction of any such well-known mark or an imitation liable to create confusion therewith. 
(2) A period of at least five years from the date of registration shall be allowed for requesting the cancellation of such a mark. The countries of the Union may provide for a period within which the prohibition of use must be requested. 
(3) No time limit shall be fixed for requesting the cancellation or the prohibition of the use of marks registered or used in bad faith." 

16. On a plain reading of the aforesaid Articles 6 and 6t`, it appears that when any person of a country of the Union for protection of his/it's mark applies for registration for same trade mark in different country(s) of the Union claiming that the said trade mark is a well known trade mark and that it has already been registered with other country or countries in the Union. In such situation, the condition for filing and registration of trade mark shall be determined in such country of the Union by its "domestics applicable law" and any country of the Union may not be refused, nor may a registration be invalidated on the ground that filing registration or renewal has not been effected in the country of origin. Such registered mark of the Union shall be deemed as "independent of mark" registered in the other country or countries of the Union, including the country of origin. In respect of well known mark, the countries of the Union undertake, if their "domestic law" so allowed or at the request of an interested party to refuse or to cancel the registration and to prohibit the use of trademark which constitutes a reproduction, an imitation, or a translation, liable to create confusion of a mark considered by the competent authority of registration or use to be well known in that different country of the Union as being already the mark of a person entitled to the benefits of this Convention and used for identical or similar goods. 

17. In the instant appeal, the appellant's trade mark "RED TAPE" admittedly was registered in India as well as the other different countries of the Union, but said trade mark has not been registered in Bangladesh. Subse-quently, application for registration of its trade mark "RED TAPE" has been submitted before the respondent No. 1, Registrar in Bangladesh being Trade Mark Application No. 137614 in Class- 25 on 14-11-2010. On the other hand, the respondent No. 3 filed application for registration trade mark "red tape" before the Registrar being Trade Mark Application No. 92081 in Class-25 on 14-6-2005. Thus, it is evident that it was filed after 5 (five) years to the respondent's application. Furthermore, the appellant has failed to produce any evidence on record before the Registrar as well as before this Court in support of its contention that the goods under the trade mark "RED TAPE" has been trading/marking in the local market in Bangladesh. The appellant has also failed to produce a single evidence before the Registrar as well as before this Court to the effect that any person of Bangladesh is importing or trading any item(s) under the trade mark "RED TAPE" or it has been exporting any class of goods in Bangladesh under the said trade mark. 

18. In view of the above position of evidence, the relevant provisions of our domestic law i.e. Trade Marks Act, 2009 is quoted below for ready reference; 
“ধারা-৮ । নিবন্ধনের বিষয়ে কতিপয় নিষেধাজ্ঞা ।--কোন মার্ক বা মার্কের অংশ ট্রেডমার্ক হিসাবে নিবন্ধিত হইবে না, যদি-
(ক) ...................... 
(খ) ................... 
(গ) উহার ব্যবহার প্রতারণামূলক হইতে পারে বা বিভ্রান্তির সৃষ্টি করিতে পারে;
(ঘ) ................. 
(ড) ................ 
(চ) ................ 
(ছ)………...
ধারা-১০। সাদৃশ্যপূর্ণ বা প্রতারণামূলকভাবে সাদৃশ্যপূর্ণ ট্রেডমার্ক নিবন্ধনে বাধা-নিষেধ ।
(১) উপ-ধারা (২) এর বিধান সাপেক্ষে, ভিন্ন কোন স্বত্বাধিকারীর নামে কোন পণ্য বা সেবা অথবা, পণ্য বা সেবার বর্ণনা নিবন্ধিত থাকিলে, উক্তরূপ পণ্য বা সেবা অথবা পণ্য বা সেবার বর্ণনার অনুরূপ বা প্রতারণামূলকভাবে সাদৃশ্যপূর্ণ কোন মার্ক নিবন্ধন করা যাইবে না।
(২) সৎ উদ্দেশ্যে যুগপৎ ব্যবহার বা অন্য কোন বিশেষ কারণে একই পণ্য বা সেবা অথবা একই বর্ণনার পণ্য বা সেবা প্রায় সাদৃশ্যপূর্ণ হইলেও উক্ত বিষয়ে কোন ট্রেডমার্ক একাধিক স্বত্বাধিকারীর নামে নিবন্ধন করা প্রয়োজন বিবেচনায় নিবন্ধক, উপযুক্ত শর্ত ও সীমাবন্ধতা সাপেক্ষে, একাধিক স্বত্মাধিকারীর নামে কোন ট্���েডমার্ক নিবন্ধনের অনুমতি দিতে পারিবেন ।
ধারা-১৬। গৃহীত আবেদন প্রত্যাখ্যান ।-কোন ট্রেডমার্ক নিবন্ধনের আবেদন গ্রহণের পর নিবন্ধক যদি এই মর্মে নিশ্চিত হন যে,
(ক) আবেদনটি ভুলবশত গৃহীত হইয়াছে; বা
(খ) ………....” 

19. Section 8(ga) provides that the Registrar cannot accept any mark or part of mark for registration, if the said mark can be registered which consists of or contents any scandalize design, or any matter use for fraud. Section 10 provides prohibition of registration of identical or similar trade mark. Sub-section (1) of section 10 provides that no trade mark shall be registered in respect of any goods or description of goods which is identical with a trade mark belonging to a different proprietor and either already on the register in respect of the same goods or description of goods or which so nearly resembles such trade mark as to be likely to deceive or cause confusion. 

20. In this regard, in the case of Abdul Motaleb and others vs Haji Aftab Miah and others reported in 16 BLT (HCD) 138, it has been held; 
"The respondent No. 1 is using the Trade Mark "Bonoful" illegally and therefore the claim of use of the Trade Mark "Bonoful" for over 14 years by the respondent hereof has no legal value and said period cannot be counted for the purpose of section 10(2) of the Trade Mark Act to get benefit as honest concurrent user and hence granting of registration of Trade Mark "Bonoful" in favour of Respondent No. 2 under section 10(2) of the Trade Marks Act is illegal."

21. In the case of Nabisco Biscuit and Bread Factory Limited, Dhaka, Appellant vs Baby Food products Limited, Dhaka and another, Respondent reported in 2008 BLD (HCD) 304, it has been observed; 
"Section 8 of the Act prohibits, inter alia, registration of any trade mark which is likely to deceive or cause confusion or otherwise be disentitled to protection in a Court of justice. Section 10 of the Act further prohibits, inter alia, registration of any trade mark which is identical with a trade mark belonging to a different proprietor and either already on the register in respect of same goods or description of goods or which so nearly resemble such trade mark as to be likely to deceive or cause confusion." 

22. Also, in the case of SM Taufiq and others-Appellants vs National Biscuit Co., New York-Respondents reported in PLD 1962 (WP) Karachi 355 (from 4th line of page No. 359) it has been held inter alia; 
"The evidence produced by the respondents undoubtedly proves that after 1940, in the territories now comprising Pakistan, the trade mark "Nabisco" was neither used nor had any reputation till 1947, or after Partition upto the time they filed application for the registration of the said trade mark." Therefore, it is found that the appellants SM Taufiq and others being the prior user, the appeal was allowed and got registration for Trade Mark "Nabisco". 

23. Considering the above provisions of law and the ratio, as settled by the apex Court, it is apparent that section 8 of the Act, 2009 prohibits registration of any trade mark or part of the mark which is likely to deceive or cause confusion and or any matter use for fraud and or otherwise be disentitled in a Court of justice. Section 10 of the Act, 2009 further prohibits registration of any trade mark which is identical with a trade mark belonging to a different proprietor and either already on the register in respect of same goods or description of goods or which so likely to deceive or cause confusion. 

24. In the instant appeal, the appellant has filed application for registration trade mark "RED TAPE" before the respondent No. 1, Registrar, which is still pending for decision by the Registrar. During pendency of the said application, the appellant had filed the opposition case against the advertisement of the respondent's trade mark "red tape" published in the Trade Marks Journal and said opposition case was rejected by the Registrar vide the impugned order and decision. However, the trade mark "RED TAPE" of the appellant has not been registered in Bangladesh under the Act, 2009 nor any class of goods under the trade mark "RED TAPE" has been marketing or is being used in the local market in Bangladesh by the appellant or any other person(s). As such, sections 8 and 10(1) of the Act, 2009 do not prohibit registration of trade mark "red tape" in favour of the respondent No.3. 

25. Countering the arguments so have been advanced by the learned Advocate for the appellant in respect of the Articles 6 and 66- is of the Paris Convention, the learned Advocate for the respondent has fortified his argument relying on the decision in the case of Samah Razor Blades Industries Ltd. vs Supermax International Pvt. Ltd. and another reported in 51 DLR 237, where it has been observed; 
"Mr Nazmul Huda, the learned Counsel drawing our attention to Article 6 of the Paris Convention, submits that the respondent can very well maintain his objection as his trade mark has been registered in India and also in various other countries and the finished product has been exported to Bangladesh and objector's right is protected under Article 6 of the said Convention. He submits that this Article indicates that the well-known trade marks may be protected under this convention to which Bangladesh is also a signatory. 
Article 6 of Paris Convention reads as follows: 
(1) Article 6(1). The countries of the Union undertake, ex-officio if their legislation so permits, or at the request of an interested party, to refuse or to cancel the registration, and to prohibit the use, of a trademark which constitutes a reproduction, an imitation, or a translation, liable to create confusion, of a mark considered by the competent authority of the country of registration or use to be well known in that country as being already the mark of a person entitled to the benefits of this convention and used for identical or similar goods. These provisions shall also apply when the essential part of the mark constitutes a reproduction of any such well-known mark or an imitation liable to create confusion therewith. 
(2) A period of at least five years from the date of registration shall be allowed for requesting the cancellation of such a mark. The countries of the Union may provide for a period within which the prohibition of use must be requested. 
(3)  ……………………” 
"It appears from this provision that this has not over-ridden any law of the country, this is in addition to the normal law of the land. We have already found that the mark of the objector-respondent was not in well-known use in this country. For attracting Article 6 of the Paris Convention there must be proof of well-known or wide use which is very much lacking in the case of the objector. Furthermore, the objector has not got his mark registered in this country. So, he now cannot claim any protection under Article 6 of the convention. Our law has not given him any right to pray for such a protection. It is also not' the case of the objector that they are exporting their products in this country after the initial ban was lifted and their products are in the market. In such a situation we find no force in the argument a situation we find no force in the argument advanced by Mr Nazmul Huda, Syed Istiaq Ahmed, the learned Counsel appearing on behalf of the appellant, raised a question whether a foreigner can bring a rectification proceeding in this country before his production is registered. Admittedly, the respondent's trade mark has not been registered in this country. They are also not exporting their products to this country. The objector is a foreigner having no factory in this country and they have also not exported their products to this country. In such a situation we find force in the argument advanced by Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed." 

26. Similar view has been taken by the High Court Division in the case of Bally Schutrabriken Ag, Switzerland vs Hosnara Begum reported in 52 DLR 546, where, it has been held; 
"From a careful review of the aforesaid decisions it appears that when a mark is opposed for registration by a foreign company on the ground that the mark is distinctive of its goods the registration of that mark and sale of such goods with that mark in foreign countries are not relevant. What is relevant in such circumstances, is the fact that the goods have been sold by the foreign company with mark thereon in the local market. In the case before us there is no record to show that the appellant has any market of this trade mark in respect of any goods in Bangladesh. Neither any sale figures were produced before the Registrar to establish the sale of "BALLY" shoes by the appellant in Bangladesh nor any other materials was placed before us to establish that the "Bally" mark of the appellant is otherwise so well known among the general public in Bangladesh the it has become a house hold word. In such situation the appellant cannot raise any objection on the registration of the mark of the respondent No.1 solely on the ground that their trade mark was registered much earlier in Switzerland and in other parts of the world. 
Mr Ohidullah submitted that although in the counter-statement the respondent No. 1 asserted that they have sold products to the tune to Taka 2,50,000 and 3,00,000 in the year 1980-81 and 1981-82 respectively/ but they have failed to produce any evidence in support thereof. In reply to this Mr Hossain contended that this matter may be decided by the Registrar in deciding the application for registration of the trade mark applied for by the respondent No.1, Mr Hossain further submitted that in the objection it has not been made an issue and, as such, in the objection case the Registrar cannot travel beyond the objection and in support thereof he relied on the decision reported in AIR 195 Cal 116 wherein it has been held that in deciding an objection the Registrar cannot go beyond the contents of the objection and, as such, the learned Registrar did not commit any illegality in rejecting the objection application as the ground taken in the objection are not tenable in law." 

27. Considering the above view so have been enunciated by the High Court Division in the case of Samah Razor Blades Industries Ltd. (supra) and Bally Schutrabriken Ag, Switzerland (supra), we are of the view that Article 61— of the Paris Convention has not overridden any law of the country and also that Convention is in addition to the domestic law of the land. If, any person of different country of the Union needs to claim benefit of such provision of the Convention in Bangladesh, it becomes his obligation to prove that the claimed trade mark is used as a well known mark in the local market in Bangladesh or the same mark has already been registered under the existing Trade Mark Act, 2009 in Bangladesh. 

28. On the other hand, the learned Advocate for the appellant has relied on the judgment in the case of Sunil Kumar Das vs Canon Kabushiki Kaisha and another reported in 2005 BLD (AD) 164 = 10 BLC (AD) 92 and 57 DLR 93, where it has been held inter alia;- 
"The mark 'CANON' with its 'LOGO' is registered in favour of respondent No. 1 in number of classes in Bangladesh and the mark is in use for the same products throughout the world. Respondent No. 1 has already acquired wide popularity goodwill and reputation in this country which establishes in the mind of the common user a connection between goods bearing Trade Mark and Respondent No. 1 and there ,is, therefore, every likelihood of deception and confusion." 

29. However, the said observation of the High Court Division has been affirmed by the Appellate Division relying on the facts that the trade mark CANON has already been registered in Bangladesh under the Trade Mark Act of Bangladesh and there was huge sale of the said brand in Bangladesh every year causing widespread publicity. Moreover, the appellant of the said appeal Mr Sunil Kumar Das applied for registration of trade mark CANON in respect of his hosiery goods long before registration of CANON in favour of the respondent Canon Kabushiki Kaisha. As such, the facts and circumstances of the present case are distinguishable. to the facts and circumstances of the cases referred by the learned Advocate for the appellant. 

30. Another contention of the learned Advocate for the appellant is that the appellant is the exclusive proprietor of the trade mark "RED TAPE" and it has been using prior to the respondent's trade mark "red tape" in the other countries of the world. In this regard, it appears from record that Mirza International Ltd. is the owner of the trade mark "RED TAPE" of A-7, Mohan Co-operation Int. Area Mathura Road, New Delhi, 110044 and it was registered in India under the existing Trade Mark Act in India. However, said mark has not been registered in Bangladesh under the existing Trade Mark Act in Bangladesh. Conversely, the trade mark "red tape" claimed by the respondent No. 3, Mr Sohel Rana, who is the sole proprietor of THA TEX of 59, B Road, Ukil Para, Narayanganj, Bangladesh and he is the sole owner of the trade mark "red tape". Thus, it is apparent that the owner of both the marks and their addresses are not same and are fully separate. Hence, such contention of the appellant is not enforceable in the eye of law. 

31. Considering the existing provisions of law and the discussions so made herein above, we have no manner of doubt to find that the appellant's trade mark "RED TAPE" is not a well known mark in Bangladesh, since, no class of goods under the said trade mark has been marketing and or is being used in the local market in Bangladesh. Furthermore, the trade mark "RED TAPE" has not been registered in this country under the Trade Mark Act in Bangladesh. On the other hand, the goods under the trade mark "red tape" has been marketing/using in the local market in Bangladesh since 2005. As such, the trade mark "red tape" of the respondent No. 3 does not constitute a reproduction, an imitation, or a translation, or liable to create confusion by the trade mark "RED TAPE" of the appellant. 
Hence, Article 66' of the Paris Convention is not applicable in the instant appeal. 

32. Last but not the least, it is appearant from record that the trade mark "RED TAPE" of the appellant was registered in India and other countries of the world and it has filed application for registration in Bangladesh on 14-11-2010 in Class 25 as well known mark. However, said application is still pending for final decision by the Registrar and also is awaiting publication in the Trade Marks Journal in Bangladesh. In view of the stated position of facts the appellant still has scope to agitate its respective grievances before the Registrar at the time of hearing of the said application for registration. 

33. Considering the facts and circumstances of the instant appeal, findings, observations and the decisions so referred herein above, we are of the view that the order and decision dated 10-1-2013 so have been passed by the respondent No. 1, Registrar rejecting the opposition case of the appellant and allowing the application for registration of trade mark "red tape" in favour of the respondent No. 3 is within the fold of law. 

34. Hence, we are not inclined to interfere with the impugned order and decision. 

35. In the result, the appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs. 

36. Communicate the judgment and order to the concerned respondents forthwith. 

Send down the Lower Court Record at once. 

End.
