full_judgment:
Borhanuddin, J: On an application under Article 102 of the Constitution filed by the petitioner this Rule has been issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the order No. 5M (9)/55-Cus (MCD)/Appeal/ Chatto/04 /918 dated 25-4-2007 (Annexure-'H') to deposit 50% of the penalty amount in cash in the appeal pending before the respondent No.1 arising out of Adjudication Order No.504 dated 8-12-2003 passed by the Respondent No.4 should not be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and why they should not be directed to hear the appeal on the basis of the bank guarantee already submitted before the respondent No.1 and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this court may seem fit and proper. 

2. Brief facts are that the petitioner is a limited company incorporated under the Companies Act and engaged in the business as shipping agent; The vessel MV SINHAI arrived at Chattogram Port on 24-5-2002 with the cargo of 151 rolls of fabrics and 72 bales of fabrics; After arrival of the ship at Chattogram Port on 24-5-2002 the vessel discharged all the containers and left the port; On 23-8-2003, respondent No.6 issued a letter of call to the petitioner relating to short-landed quantity of 1 roll of fabric and readymade garments and 51 bales of cotton fabrics; The petitioner duly submitted his explanation; Respondent No.4 without considering explanation of the petitioner arbitrarily imposed a penalty of Taka 25,32,567 for the short-landed garments and fabrics vide adjudication order dated 10-12-2003; 

3. Being aggrieved, the petitioner preferred appeal under section 193 of the Customs Act and filed an application under section 194 of the Customs Act praying for dispensation of the penalty amount before hearing of the appeal. Respondent No.3 registrar on behalf of the respondent No.1 Commissioner of Customs vide its letter dated 30-3-2004 asked the petitioner to deposit the penalty amount by way of 50% in cash and 50% bank guarantee. Due to financial hardship and for not holding fund from its principal the petitioner in response to the notice dated 30-3-2004 through its advocates' letter dated 22-6-2005 submitted before the respondent No. 4 a bank guarantee dated 21-6-2005 issued by Standard Chartered Bank, Sheikh Mujib Road, Chattogram, covering the entire penalty amount in favour of the respondent No.1 before hearing of the appeal. Respondent No.3 vide letter dated 27-3-2007 again asked the petitioner to deposit 50% of the penalty amount in cash and 50% of the penalty amount by way of bank guarantee. Petitioner vide letter dated 29-3-2007 requested the respondent No.1 to fix a date of hearing of the appeal as bank guarantee covering the entire penalty amount has been furnished. But the respondent No.1 without giving any opportunity of hearing for acceptance of the bank guarantee covering entire penalty amount vide letter dated 25-4-2007 intimated the petitioner that since 100% of the penalty amount has been deposited by way of bank guarantee the appeal cannot be accepted for hearing. 

4. Having aggrieved by and dissatisfied, the petitioner moved this application under Article 102 of the Constitution and obtained the present Rule alongwith an order of stay. 

5. Mr Muhammad Ohiullah, learned advocate appearing for the petitioner submits that since financial hardship was asserted on behalf of the petitioner and a bank guarantee has been submitted by the petitioner covering entire penalty amount, the respondents ought to have accepted the same in exercise of the discretion vested upon them by 2nd proviso of section 194 of the Customs Act, but inspite of exercising discretionary power and without giving an opportunity of hearing, the respondents most illegally and arbitrarily refused to entertain the appeal for not depositing 50% in cash and 50% bank guarantee ignoring the fact that the petitioner is a mere agent of the vessel who does not hold any fund from the principal as well as the very fact of financial hardship as ascertained by the petitioner by filing application under section 194 of the customs Act. Referring to the case of Rainbow Shipping Lines vs Collector of Customs, reported in 53 DLR 408, the case of Seacom Shipping Ltd. vs Commissioner of Customs, 6 BLC 576, the case of Sentrans Maritime (BD) Limited vs The Commissioner of Customs, 6 MLR (2001) 249, the case of Ocean Trade Ltd. vs The Commissioner of Customs, Excise and VAT, 11 BLT (2003) 438, the case of Pacific Ocean Lines vs Government of Bangladesh & others, 68 DLR 446 and an unreported judgment passed by this Division in Writ Petition No.9033 of 2006 with Writ Petition No.9034 of 2006 (United Shipping Lines, vs The Commissioner of Customs, Excise and VAT (Appeal), Mr Ohiullah submits that in a number of cases similar issue of filing appeal before the commissioner of customs on furnishing 100% bank guarantee covering entire penalty amount was raised and settled by this court and since the petitioner standing on the same footing it's case may be dealt with in the like manner. He lastly submits that impugned order of the respondent No. 1 in refusing to entertain the appeal after submit-ting 100% bank guarantee by the petitioner covering entire penalty amount is violative of amended section 194 of the Customs Act as amended in the year 2004 through Finance Act, 2004 (Act No.16 of 2004). 

6. On the other hand, Mr Pratikar Chakma learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the respondent by filing affidavit-in-opposition submits that the 2nd Proviso of section 194 of the Customs Act vested a discretionary power to the appellate authority  to decide hardship. In support of his submission, learned Deputy Attorney-General referred an unreported judgment passed by this Division in Writ Petition No. 12424 of 2017 alongwith 11 writ petitions as well as another unreported judgment passed in Writ Petition No.7261 of 2018 [Trouser World (Pvt.) Ltd. vs Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal and another]. 

7. Heard learned advocate for the petitioner and learned Deputy Attorney-General for the respondent. Perused the writ petition and the annexures appended thereof. 

8. Admittedly the petitioner is a shipping agent of the vessel MV SINHAI which was penalized by the Customs Authority for short-landing vide adjudicating authority of the commissioner of customs. Against the adjudication order the petitioner preferred appeal before the Commissioner of Customs, Excise and VAT (Appeal) Chattogram and filed an application under section 194 of the Customs Act wherein the petitioner categorically asserted its financial hardship and thereafter submitted 100% bank guarantee covering entire penalty amount. From the impugned order (Annexure-'H' to the writ petition) it does not transpires that the respondent appellate authority considered the application under section 194 filed by the petitioner. Though the petitioner furnished 100% bank guarantee for the entire penalty amount but the respondent refused to accept the appeal for statutory deposit of 50% in cash and 50% bank guarantee though statute empowers the appellate authority to exercise discretionary power in case of hardship. 

9. For better appreciation, section 194 of the Customs Act prevailing at the relevant period is reproduced below: 
"194. Deposit, Pending appeal, of duty demanded or penalty levied.—(1) Any person desirous of appealing under section 193 or section 196A against any decision or order relating to any duty demanded in respect of goods which have ceased to be under the control of customs authorities or to any penalty levied under this Act shall, at the time of filing his appeal or if he is so permitted by the appellate authority at any later stage before the consideration of the appeal, deposit with the appropriate officer fifty percent of the duty demanded or fifty percent of the penalty imposed, or both, as the case may be: 
Provided that such person may, instead of depositing the amount of the penalty as aforesaid deposit only fifty percent thereof and furnish a guarantee from a scheduled bank for the due payment of the balance; 
Provided further that where, in any particular case, the appellate authority is of the opinion that the deposit of duty demanded or penalty imposed will cause undue hardship to the appellant, if may dispense with such deposit, either unconditionally or subject to such conditions as it may deem fit to impose. 
(2) …………..”

10. Though the provision of section 194 prevailing at the relevant period provides to deposit 50% of the duty demanded or 50% of the penalty imposed but the respondent demanded 100% of the penalty amount by depositing 50% in cash and 50% in bank guarantee which is contrary to the provisions of law prevailing at the relevant time and clearly shows that the respondent failed to apply its judicial mind in passing the impugned order. 

11. We have also perused the judgment passed by a larger Bench in Writ Petition No.12424 of 2017 alongwith other 11 writ petitions. 12. In the concluding portion of the judgment their lordships held that:
"When a Tribunal is set up under an Act for adjudicating the disputes between the contending sides relating to the rights and privileges conferred under the Act, unless otherwise provided by law, the jurisdiction of the Tribunal is exclusive. However, this should not be inferred as a total ouster of the Court's jurisdiction. Where the Tribunal exceeds its authority or where it fails to exercise its power in accordance with law or where it has acted malafide, in such cases, this Court can and should interfere." 

13. In the case in hand, it appears that though the petitioner furnished 100% bank guarantee covering entire penalty amount and also filed an application under section 194 narrating the cause of hardship but the respondent appellate authority did not consider the application filed by the petitioner under section 194, even did not afford an opportunity of hearing to the petitioner, rather passed the impugned order based on earlier provision of section 194 of the Customs Act without considering the amended provision prevailing at the relevant time. It also appears from the judgment referred by learned Deputy Attorney-General that the jurisdiction of this court is not totally ousted by the larger Bench. 

14. We have also perused another judgment referred by the learned Deputy Attorney-General passed in Writ Petition No.7261 of 2018. Facts of the case is different from the case in hand inasmuch as in that case the application filed by the petitioner under section 194(1) of the Customs Act was taken up by the Tribunal and after hearing the parties allowed the application directing the petitioner to deposit 10% in cash and furnish bank guarantee for further 10% of the amount of duty so demanded. But in the instant case though the petitioner filed application under section 194 asserting cause of hardship and furnished 100% bank guarantee covering entire penalty amount but the respondent did not afford any opportunity of hearing to the petitioner and did riot consider the hardship at all. 

15. On reading the provision of section 194 of the Customs Act it appears that both 1st proviso and 2nd proviso of section 194 of the Customs Act given discretion upon the Customs Authority to consider the hardship of the appellant. Since the petitioner filed application under section 194 asserting hardship and furnish 100% bank guarantee for the entire penalty amount, the respondent No.1 would have exercise its jurisdiction by accepting the said bank guarantee. Discretion does not mean arbitrary exercise of power rather discretion have to apply judiciously considering application filed by the appellant concern under section 194 of the Customs Act. 

16. From the discussions made above, we are of the view that the respondent passed the order refusing to accept the appeal of the petitioner illegally without invoking amended provision of law prevailing at the relevant period and without considering hardship asserted by the petitioner in accordance with law. 

17. In the result, the Rule is made absolute. 

18. No order as to cost. 

19. The impugned order dated 25-4-2007 is hereby set-aside and the respondent No.1 is directed to hear the appeal accepting 100% bank guarantee furnished by the petitioner covering entire amount of penalty within 3(three) months from the date of-receipt of this judgment. 

Order of stay granted at the time of issuance of the Rule and extended from time to time is hereby vacated. 

End.

lawyer:
MA Azim Khair with Md Sultanuzzaman (Sumon), Advocates—For the Petitioners.

Md Nazmul Huda, Advocate—For the Opposite-Parties.
parties:
Kafil Uddin (Md) being dead his heirs Md Anowar Hossain and others ------- Petitioners
vs
Md Abdul Gani and others ---------- Opposite parties
full_judgment:
In this revisional application Rule has been issued calling upon the opposite party Nos.1-2 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 17-9-1991 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Gaibandha in other Class Appeal No. 161 of 1986 should not be se-aside and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

2. Kafil Uddin, since deceased, as plaintiff filed Other Class Suit No. 97 of 1984 in the Court of learned Munsif (Now Assistant Judge), Sadar, Gaibandha for partition of the suit property impleading opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 and others as defendants. 

3. The plaint case, in short, is that the suit land originally belonged to Banu Sheikh and Kukra Sheikh in equal shares, Banu Sheikh died leaving two sons namely Saimuddin and Afaz Uddin and one daughter namely Khotekjan; Saimuddin and Afaz Uddin transferred their share in favour of their respective wives namely Bachani Bibi and Kaich Bibi by registered sale deed being No. 1792 dated 2-2-1959 and delivered possession thereof. While Bachani and Kaich Bibi were possessing the said land, they transferred 36 decimals of land of Plot No. 6798 to the plaintiff by a registered sale deed dated 10-10-1964; on the same day, the plaintiff also executed and registered a deed of re-conveyance in favour of them promising to re-convey the property to them if the vendor pay back the consideration money within 5 years; but the vendor did not pay back the consideration money within the said period; consequently, the sale deed became absolute and the plaintiff has been in possession of his purchased land as absolute owner; as the plaintiff faced difficulty in continuing with the ejmali possession, the plaintiff sought partition to the co sharers and being refused, compelled to file the suit. 

4. Opposite party Nos. 1 & 2, as defendant nos. 1 & 2, contested the suit by filing written statement denying material allegations of the plaint and contended, inter alia, that by Kabala dated 10-10-1964 Bachani Bibi and Kaich Bibi in fact mortgaged the property for a period of 5 years and after the expiry of said 5 years Bachani and Kaich Bibi got back the property in accordance with the provision of President's Order No. 88 of 1972; Bachani Bibi and Kaich Bibi, after getting back the property, while possessing the same, sold the same along with other land, to the defendant No. 1 & 2 by registered sale deed dated 10-3-1975, 19-5-1975, 5-2-1974, 3-8-1977 and 10-3-1975. The plaintiff has no right, title and interest in the suit land; they sought for separate saham for their purchased land. 

5. After hearing, the trial Court decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiffs on the analogy that Bacani Bibi and Kaich Bibi transferred 36 decimals of lands to the plaintiff on 10-10-1964 with condition that the said land will be retransferred to them if they repay the price within 5 years, but the defendants failed to prove that they get the property redeemed as usufructuary mortgage within the stipulated time and the conditional sale by them to the plaintiff became absolute with expiry of 5 years. The trial Court further held that the transaction became 'past and closed' in 1969 and shall not come within the purview of usufructuary mortgage. The trial Court held that as the transaction is 'past and closed' in 1969, it will not come under the purview of President Order No. 88 of 1972. 

6. The appellate court reversed the findings of the trial court and dismissed the suit holding that, 
i) Upon an application made under the provision of President's Order No. 88 of 1972, the appellant got an order on 10-6-1987 in Miscellaneous Case No. 119 of 1986 for returning of the suit property, and hence the plaintiff failed to prove his case; 
ii) The decision reported in 34 DLR (AD) 237 is applicable in the instant case. 

7. Mr MA Azim Khair learned advocate appearing for the petitioner submits that, the conditional sale deed turned into absolute deed of sale by operation of law as per condition stipulated in the agreement which expired in 1969 before promulgation of President's Order No. 88 of 1972 but the appellate court failed to advert that vital aspect of the case and erroneously reversed the findings of the trial court which caused failure of Justice. Learned Advocate next submits that the transaction in the instant case became "Past & Closed" which will not come within the purview of President's Order No. 88 of 1972 and, as such, the transaction in question will not be usufructuary mortgage in respect of plaintiffs' 36 decimal land. Learned advocate further submits that the appellate court erroneously relied upon the decision reported in 34 DLR (AD) 237 which will not be applicable given the facts and circumstances of the instant case, rather the principle enunciated in 32 DLR (AD) 233 will be applicable in the instant case which has been consistently followed in some other decisions viz 1996 BLD (AD) 210 = 1 BLC (AD) 90, 48 DLR 25, 49 DLR (AD) 48 and 1 BLC (AD) 90 and, as such, judgment and decree passed by the appellate court is not sustainable. Learned Advocate lastly submits that the plaintiff much earlier filed other class suit No. 97 of 1984 before the court of Munsif, Sadar, Gaibandha now Assistant Judge, Sadar, Gaibandha, for partition of the suit land impleading the present opposite party No. 1 & 2 as defendants and the said suit was decreed on 13-9-1986 but the defendants initiated Miscellaneous Case No. 119 of 1986 before the Magistrate, Gaibandha much later who were parties to the other class suit No. 97 of 1984 and the magistrate passed order on 10-6-1987 knowing fully well about that judgment and decree passed earlier by the civil court and, as such, the order dated 10-6-1987 is not sustainable. 

8. On the other hand, Mr Md Nazmul Huda learned advocate appearing for the opposite-party submits that upon an application made under the provision of President's Order No. 88 of 1972, the opposite parties defendants got order on 10-6-1987 Miscellaneous Case No. 119 of 1986 for returning of the suit property treating the same as usufructuary mortgage and considering the facts and circumstances the appellate court rightly reversed the judgment and decree of the trial court and dismissed the suit and, as such, the instant revisional application has no merit. Learned Advocate next submits that, proper forum to file application for returning the land in respect of a deed regarding conditional sale is concerned magistrate and, as such, the defendant opposite parties by filing application to the said forum vide Miscellaneous Case No. 119 of 1986 got order of the suit land treating as usufructuary mortgage and, as such, the present Rule has no merit. Learned Advocate submits that, the decision reported the 34 DLR (AD) 237 is applicable in the facts and circumstances of the instant case and, as such, the contention of the petitioner is not sustainable. Learned Advocate lastly submits that, the appellate court as last court of facts allowed the appeal considering facts and circumstances of the case and, as such, Judgment and decree of the appellate court is not liable to be reversed. 

9. Having perused the pleadings and other materials it appears that, prior to coming into force of President's Order No. 88 of 1972, a transaction by way of out and out sale coupled with an agreement for re-conveyance by itself, does not constitute as complete usufructuary mortgage but after promulgation of President's Order No. 88 of 1972 on 3-8-1972 section 95A was incorporated in the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which is as follows : 
"95A.—Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, any transfer of a holding or of a portion or share thereof, where the transferor receives from the transferee any consideration and the transferee acquires the right to possess, and to enjoy the usufruct of such holding or portion or share thereof for a specified period in lieu of such consideration, shall notwithstanding any-thing contained in the document relating to the transfer, be deemed to be a complete usufructuary mortgage for a period not exceeding seven years and the provisions of Section 95 shall apply to such transfer whether made before or after the date of commencement of the State Acquisition and Tenancy (Second Amendment) Order, 1972." 

10. Subsequently, by President's Order No. 136 of 1972 the section 95A was amended and after the words and comma "any transfer of a holding or of a portion or share thereof" incorporated the following phrase "either by way of an out and out sale with an agreement to re-convey" and thereby such transaction brought within the mischief of complete usufructuary mortgage. 

11. Thereafter by President's Order No. 24 of 1973, sub-section (4) and (5) of section 95 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was substituted. 

12. In the instant .case, as the transaction took place on 10-10-1964 for a period of 5 years, the said period of 5 years expired on 10-10-1969 and, as such, at the time of promulgation of President's Order No. 88 of 1972, the said transaction was concluded as 'Past and Closed' and therefore, the trial court appreciating the spirit of law rightly held that the transaction in question does not come within the mischief of President's Order No. 88 of 1972. The said principle has been nicely expounded in 32 DLR (AD) 233 which is hereunder : 
"Those transactions which are subsisting on the date of promulgation of President's Order No. 88 of 1972 are hit by section 95A including the transaction entered into by way of an out and out sale with an agreement to reconvey, made whether before or after the promulgation of President's Order No. 88 of 1972 and (5) as for the transactions which are not alive before the promulgation of President's Order No. 88 of 1972 they are concluded by the transaction past and closed." 

13. The said decision is subsequently followed in many cases reported in 16 BLD AD 210, 48 DLR 25; 49 DLR (AD) 48, 49 DLR 172 and 1 BLC (AD) 90. So it is now well settled that the transaction which took place before the pro-mulgation of President's Order No. 88 of 1972 but not alive at the time of promulgation of President's Order No. 88 of 1972 are concluded by the transaction "Past and closed". 

14. The court of appeal below without taking notice of the observation as mentioned above erroneously relied upon the decision reported in 34 DLR (AD) 237 and held that the transaction in question is complete usufructuary mortgage and the property automatically returned back to the Bachani Bibi and others in accordance with the provision of President's Order No. 88 of 1972. In a reported decision at 34 DLR (AD) 237, the plaintiff filed the suit in civil court for redemption of suit land claiming the transaction in question as a Kot-mortgage wherein the concept 'past and closed' was not debated and resolved. The instant case is relating to a transaction with an agreement for 5 years and before promulgation of PO No. 88 of 1972 the term of the separate agreement having expired it will not come within the ambit of PO No. 88 of 1972 and, as such, the decision reported in 34 DLR (AD) 237 is clearly distinguishable. 

15. The court of appeal below further relying on order dated 10-6-1987 passed by Magistrate, Gaibandha in Petition Case No. 119 of 1986 held that the defendant appellant obtained an order for return of the suit land but the fact of filing Petition Case before the Upazila Magistrate or obtaining order of returning back of the suit land is beyond pleading and the said order was not brought into record by way of adducing additional evidence and, as such, the appellate court's such finding is not tenable. 

16. It appears that, Title Suit No. 97 of 1984 was filed much earlier and the trial court decreed the suit on 13-9-1986 therefore, the learned Magistrate was bound by the decree of the civil court, but defying the decree of the civil court the learned Magistrate passed the order on 10-6-1987 in Petition Case No. 119 of 1986 which is palpably illegal hence finding of the appellate court relying upon such order is not sustainable. 

17. In the above facts and circumstances, I find merit in the Rule and accordingly the Rule is made absolute. 

18. The judgment and decree dated 17-9-1991 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Gaibandha in other Class Appeal No. 161 of 1986 is hereby se-aside and the judgment and decree dated 13-9-1986 passed by the Court of learned Munsif (Now Assistant Judge), Sadar, Gaibandha in Other Class Suit No. 97 of 1984 is hereby upheld. 

19. No order as to costs. 

20. The order of stay granted at the time of issuance of the Rule and extended time to time is hereby recalled and vacated. 

Send down the lower courts' records. 

End.

lawyer:
Sherder Abul Hossain, Advocate—For the Petitioner.

MM Shafiullah, Advocate—For the Opposite Party Nos. 1(a) to 1(m).
parties:
Tusta Chandra Mandal  Plaintiff-Appellant-------- Petitioner
vs
Samsul Haque being dead his legal heirs-Nur Mohammad and others Defendant -Respondent------Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule has been issued, calling upon the opposite parties, to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 10-4-2014 (decree signed on 15-4-2014), passed by the Joint District Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka, in Title Appeal No.135 of 2004, dismissing the appeal and thereby affirming the judgment and decree dated 10-4-2004 (decree signed on 17-4-2004), passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Savar, Dhaka, in Title Suit No.36 of 2002, should not be set-aside and/or pass such other order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

2. Facts, relevant for disposal of the Rule, in brief, are that one Sree Tusta Chandra Mandal son of late Rakhal Chandra Mandal, as plaintiff, had filed Title Suit No.36 of 2002, on 6-1-2002, before the court of Senior Assistant Judge, Savar, Dhaka, against Shamsul Haque and others, with a prayer for declaration that, the plaintiff is the owner of 16 annas property, as described in the schedule "Ka" to the plaint, and that the deed Nos. 5067, 5069 and 5071 registered in the office of the Sub-Registrar, Savar and the deed Nos. 3038 and 3039 regigtered in the office of the Sub-Registrar, Kalampur, Dhamrai, Dhaka, were forged, fabricated and by that deeds, the plaintiff's title in the suit property has not been affected in any manner. All these deeds were registered on 3-6-1981. Moreover, the plaintiff has described his case in his plaint as well as at paragraph No.2 of the revisional application. I have gone through the facts narrated in the plaint, which need not be repeated here for the sake of brevity.

3. The defendant No. 1 appeared and con-tested in this suit by filing written statements, on 11-11-2002, in which, he has specifically denied all material allegations made in the plaint and has stated his own case at paragraph Nos. "L" to "Y" of the written statements. I have also gone through the facts stated in the written statement, which need not be repeated here for the sake of brevity. 

4. The plaintiff had examined 3 witnesses before the trial court, including himself, namely—PWs 1-3, to prove his case and had produced and proved certain documents which were marked as Exhibit 1 to 1(Gha). On the other hand, the defendants had examined 5 witnesses before the trial court where the defendant No. 1 had examined himself as DW 1 and other witnesses deposed as DWs 2-5. Besides, the defendant had produced and proved certain documents marked as Exhibit “ক” to “ত”

5. The trial court, after hearing the parties and having assessed the evidence on record, by its judgment and decree dated 10-4-2004 (decree signed on 17-4-2004) had dismissed the suit. 

6. Against the said judgment and decree of the trial court, the plaintiff preferred Title Appeal No.135 of 2004, before the District Judge, Dhaka, which was heard by the Joint District Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka. In appeal, the plaintiff has given additional evidence by adducing his mother (defendant No. 7), who has deposed before the appellate court as PW On the other hand, the defendants have also given additional evidence before the appellate court, by producing one Poresh Chandra Mondal and Md Amir Uddin (DW 6 and 7), being the attesting witnesses of the questioned documents. After hearing the parties and having considered the evidence on record, the appellate court concurred with the findings of the trial court and has dismissed the appeal, thereby it has affirmed the judgment and decree of the trial court, vide its judgment and decree dated 10-4-2014 (decree signed on 15-4-2014). 

7. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the said judgment and decree of the appellate court, the plaintiff-appellant, as petitioner, filed this application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, and obtained the instant Rule. 

8. During pendency of the Rule, the opposite party No. 1 died and his heirs were duly substituted as opposite party Nos. 1(a) to 1(m), as per order dated 13-11-2018 of this Court. 

9. Learned Advocate Mr Sherder Abul Hossain appeared on behalf of the petitioner. He, having placed the revisional application and other materials on record, mainly submits that, admittedly Rakhal Chandra Mondal was the owner of 16 annas (the entire) suit property and he died leaving his wife Laxmi Bewa and the plaintiff Sree Tusta Chandra Mandal, as owners of the suit property. He next points out that, the plaintiff was minor, therefore, he had no knowledge about the 5 sale deeds described in the schedule "Kha" to the plaint. He proceeds on that, the defendants had created those forged documents. However, the plaintiff had to file Title Suit No.38 of 2000 seeking permanent injunction against the defendants and the defendants filed written statements in that suit, claiming title in the suit property alleging that, the suit property was sold to them, by the plaintiff's mother as his guardian, appointed in the Guardianship Case No.1316 of 1980 and that she had also obtained sale permission on 3-1-1984. The learned Advocate next submits that, the plaintiff has thus come to know about these 5 disputed sale deeds and had filed the instant suit seeking declaration of his title as owner of 16 annas of the suit property as well as for further declaration that the aforesaid 5 deeds were forged, fabricated and not binding upon him. The learned Advocate, having drawn my attention to the documents maintained in the LCR, continues that, in the Guardianship Case, name of Laxmi Bewa appears only as petitioner and there is no name of any respondents, vide Exhibit "Da". He next refers to the certified copy of the Suit Register of Permission Miscellaneous Case No. 1688 of 1980 and submits that, it does not prove that Laxmi Bewa had filed this case or that she got permission to sell the suit property. Therefore, the sale to the defendants was not valid and all these documents were obtained by resorting to fraud and forgery by the defendants. He also submits that, the defendants were not in possession of the suit property, while the DW 1, who was borgader, has proved the plaintiffs possession in the suit property. But, this has not been taken into consideration by the courts below. He next submits that, this is a case where the validity of the disputed sale deeds has been challenged on the ground of forgery, but not on the execution of these disputed documents by a validly appointed guardian in as much as the plaintiff does not admit appointment of his mother Laxmi Bawa as his guardian. Therefore, this case should fall under Article 120 Schedule- I of the Limitation Act, 1908, not under Article 44 Schedule- 1 of the said Act. He, therefore, submits that, both the courts below ought to have held that, the suit was not barred by limitation as per Article 44 of the Limitation Act, 1908. As such, he sums up that, the courts below have committed grave error of law and that has resulted in error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. He concludes that, this Rule has merit and the same may kindly be made absolute. 

10. On the contrary, Mr MM Shafiullah, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite party Nos. 1(a) to 1(m) submits that, the plaintiff's mother, who was the defendant No. 7 before the court below, in this suit filed by the plaintiff (her son), but she herself did not file this suit questing the validity of the sale deeds described in schedule "Kha" to the plaint, nor had she appeared in the trial court to support the plaintiff's case. She has appeared as an witness for the plaintiff-appellant in Title Appeal No. 135 of 2004. He next refers to the deposition of Laxmi Bewa (mother of the plaintiff) wherein she has deposed (before the appellate court) that, “আমি আমার নাবালক পুত্রদ্বয়ের অভিভাবক হওয়ার জন্য জেলা জজ আদালতে ১৩১৬/৮০ নম্বর মামলা করেছিলাম । এই মামলায় আমি অভিভাবক নিযুক্ত হয়েছিলাম । আমার অভিভাবক নিযুক্ত আদেশ বিজ্ঞ জেলা জজ আদালত বাতিল করেন নাই।” Next referring to the said deposition the learned Advocate also points out that, during cross examination, this deponent has admitted before the appellate court that, “সাভারে দলিল করিয়া দিয়াছি। উহা বাদীকে বলি নাই । বাদী আমার পুত্র হয় ।”The learned Advocate further submits that, this admission of Laxmi Bewa, considered alongwith the deposition of defendant's witnesses and the documents proved by them, it is apparent that, the depositions of witnesses of the defendants have been corroborated by the plaintiff's mother. The fact that she had executed the aforesaid 5 sale deeds, as guardian of the minors and for the benefit of the minors, i.e for purchasing another house by the sale proceeds of the aforesaid kabala deeds, has also been proved, the learned Advocate also adds to his submission. Next, referring to the Suit Register of the Guardian-ship Case No. 1316 of 1980 (Exhibit "Da"), the learned Advocate for the opposite party submits that, the name of the petitioner alone will appear in the said case in as much as none else had contested for guardianship of the minors. There was no objection to her prayer for the guardianship, hence, there was no name in the column of respondent, in the suit register of the Guardianship Case). But, the learned Advocate for the petitioner has misinterpreted this document, before this Court, he further submits. The learned Advocate for the opposite party Nos. 1(a) to 1(m) also submits that, Laxmi Bewa, the mother of the plaintiff, was appointed as guardian of the minors plaintiff and the fact of the execution of the aforesaid 5 sale deeds were proved, as per provisions of section 68 of the Evidence Act, 1872, by producing the attesting witnesses, before the appellate court. Besides, he argues that, the plaintiff did not file this suit within 3 years after attaining majority i.e. before expiry of 1999, rather he has filed the suit on 7-2-2002, that is long after expiry of the period prescribed in Article 44, schedule 1 of the Limitation Act, 1908. The learned Advocate for the opposite party empathically submits that, since an appointment of guardianship has been proved by adequate evidence, therefore, the submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioner that the period of limitation shall be counted under Article 120, schedule 1 of the Limitation Act, 1908, is not correct. The learned Advocate also submits that, since the plaintiff's mother (defendant No. 7) had executed the questioned documents (Exhibit Gha series) therefore, she did not appear before the trial court to give deposition in favour of the plaintiff. This conduct of the executant Laxmi Bewa also proves that she had executed the aforesaid 5 sale deeds, while she has admitted that she has executed the 3 deeds in the office of the Sub-Registrar, Savar namely deed Nos. 5067, 5069 and 5071, although she had denied the execution of deed Nos. 3038 and 3039 in the office of the Sub-Registrar, Kalampur, Dhamrai, Dhaka. He proceeds on that, the defendants have proved execution of all the 5 deeds, by producing 2 attesting witnesses. 

11. At this stage, the learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that, execution of 5 deeds in the office of 2 different Sub-Registrar's Office on the same date i.e. on 3-6-1981, proved that, the defendants have resorted to fraud and forgery in executing these deeds. Otherwise, he submits, why the executant should execute and register the deed Nos. 3038 and 3029 in the office of the Sub-Registrar, Kalampur, Dhamrai, Dhaka, although the property is situated within the jurisdiction of Savar Sub-Registrar office. In reply to this submission, the learned Advocate for the opposite party argues that, as per section 28 of the Registration Act, execution of these 2 deeds at Kalampur Sub-Registrar Office was permitted by law (at that line) and in support of his contention he has referred to 37 DLR (AD) 177: Syed Kawsar Ali vs Gahar Kazi and others. Besides, the learned Advocate for the opposite party submits that, the case of the defendant has duly been proved by submitting relevant DCR, mutation khatian, Khajna Dhakilas etc. and as well as the defendants have submitted all 5 original kabala deeds and all these were duly proved and were marked as exhibits by the trial court. He next refers to the examination of DW 4, Hazi Habibur Rahman, who has deposed in the trial court stating that, there was a dispute between the defendants and one Helal Uddin, who purchased some property of the deceased Rakhal Chandra Mondal from his second wife Sagor Bewa (Step-mother of the plaintiff) and a complaint case was filed before the Martial Law Court in the year 1982 and the dispute was referred to the Savar Union Parishad and the Union Parishad had resolved the dispute in an amicable settlement and the defendants got 1.83 decimals of land. As such, it will be evident from the evidence on record, in all the forums and in all cases, including the case filed for permanent injunction and before the Martial Law Court, the defendants have appeared and contested to protect their title in the suit property, since they are the bonafide purchaser for value. He next submits that, in cross examination of the deposition of Laxmi Bewa, she was asked as to whether she was willing to sent her thumb impression for expert opinion, but she did not sent the same, although she had agreed to sent, because if the same were sent for expert opinion, then it would have been revealed that she herself had executed all these disputed 5 sale deeds. He therefore, concludes that, this Rule has no merit and the same may kindly be discharged. 

12. I have heard the learned Advocates for both the parties, perused the impugned judgments as well as pleadings of the parties, the evidences and other materials on record. 

13. I find that, the plaintiff's mother, who was the defendant No. 7, before the court below, has appeared as witness for the plaintiff-appellant in Title Appeal No. 135 of 2004, where she has admitted that, she had applied for appointment of guardianship of the minor plaintiff, vide Guardianship Case No. 1316 of 1980 and was appointed as guardian of the said minors. Her guardianship was not cancelled by the district court, she also admits. Although she had in the same breath deposed that, her guardianship was cancelled in a Miscellaneous Case No. 53 of 1981, but no such document was either filed by her, nor by the plaintiff-appellant. 

14. Having considered the argument of both sides, regarding Suit Register of the Guardianship Case No. 1316 of 1980 (Exhibit "Da"), I find that, the name of Laxmi Bewa has been recorded as the applicant in the said suit register. As no one else had contested for the guardianship of the minors, therefore, there was no name in the column of respondent, in that register. Hence, this point has been duly clarified by the learned Advocate for the opposite party Nos. 1(a) to 1(m), in the course of his submission. 

15. Having considered the deposition of the defendant's witnesses, as recorded by the trial court as well as of two other DWs, who have deposed before the appellate court as the attesting witnesses, I find that the defendants have produced the 5 disputed sale deeds in original and proved all 5 title deeds before the trial court, marked as Exhibit "Gha" series. They have also placed and proved all these relevant documents connected to the sale. I also find that Poresh Chandra Mondal and Amir Uddin, who deposed as attesting witnesses before the appellate court, are attesting witnesses in all 5 documents and they have testified consistently about execution of these 5 deeds by Laxmi Bewa and the minor discrepancy that was found in the deposition of Amir Uddin (as regards the Registration Office) was not material, in as much as, due to elapse of a long time, the attesting witness Amir Uddin might have forgotten if these deeds were registered in one or two Sub-Registrar's Office. Moreso, when this is a matter of documentary evidence and this deponent could have given the name of both Sub-Registrars Offices by refreshing his memory. However, no material inconsistency has been found in their deposition. Besides, the documentary evidence as proved and marked as Exhibit-K to Z, clearly consistently and adequately proved the defendant's title and possession in the suit property, since the date of their purchase subject, however, to obtaining the sale permission. 

16. On the contrary, the plaintiff's oral evidence are not supported by any documen-tary evidence, like Khatian or Khajna Dakhila and he has utterly failed to discharge the burden of proof that rested on him. Besides, as has been rightly pointed out by the trial court, and concurred with by the appellate court, the plaintiff has falsely claimed that he was in possession of the suit property. It was found by both the courts bellow that, the plaintiff's suit was liable to be dismissed under the provisions of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877, for not seeking consequential relief by way of recovery of khas possession, which is, in my considered opinion, is correct opinion of the courts below. 

17. Moreover, refusal of Laxmi Bewa to send her thumb impression for examination by finger-print expert, also leads to an adverse presumption against her as per provisions of section 114(g) of the Evidence Act, 1872. 

18. The plaintiff did not file this suit within 3 years of his attainment of majority i.e. before expiry of 1999. He has filed the suit on 7-2-2002. The guardianship of Laxmi Bewa being proved, his suit falls under and is barred by Article 44, Schedule-1 of the Limitation Act, 1908. 

19. Since, the appointment of guardianship has been admitted by Laxmi Bewa and has also been proved by adequate evidence, therefore, the submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioner that the limitation period shall be counted under Article 120 of Schedule-1 of the Limitation Act, 1908, is of no substance. 

20. The vital defect in this case was the failure of the defendant to produce the sale permission. In each cases, in order to lawfully and effectively transfer the property of a minor, the executants should not only be appointed as guardian of the person and property of the minor is concerned, but he/she should also have sale permission for transferring the minor's property or otherwise to enter into any deal with the minor's movable or immovable property in question. 

21. As such, although this ground was available to the plaintiff, he has, however, lost this opportunity, since he did not admit guardianship of his mother or the execution of the questioned deeds by his guardian, rather he has tried to make out a case that the said deeds were not executed by his mother, rather these deeds were created by fraud and forgery, by the defendants. So, he could not take the ground that there was no sale permission, while his suit is hopelessly barred by limitation prescribed under Article 44 of the 1st schedule of the Limitation Act, 1908, in as much as the case of guardianship has been proved as well as admitted by Laxmi Bewa herself. Similarly view was taken in the case reported in 14 BLT 
519: Md Anwar Hossain vs Md Lal Miah. 

22. Moreover, it has to be made clear that, in the absence of permission to sell the property of the minor, the sale is voidable, but not void, as per provisions of section 30 of the Guardianship Act and in the instant case, all the deeds were voidable for want of permission duly obtained. But, in order to declare these 5 deeds void, the plaintiff ought to have filed a suit before expiry of 1999 i.e. before expiry of 3 years of attaining majority as per Article 44 of the Limitation Act, which he had failed to do. 

23. As regards execution of two sets of document in two Sub-Registrar's Offices, although the properties were is situated within the jurisdiction of Savar Sub-Registrar office, I am of the opinion that, at the relevant time, as per provisions of section 28(2) of the Registration Act, 1908, execution of these 2 deeds at two different Sub-Registrar's Offices were permissible by law and this fact does not, by itself, negates the fact of execution of the deeds, the execution having been duly proved by the attesting witnesses as well as corroborated by the fact of delivery of possession and creation of the mutation khatin, separation of Jama and Khajna Dakhila etc. duly produced and proved before the court below. 

24. However, I find substance in the sub-mission of the learned Advocate for the petitioner that, in a clear case of forgery of document, the provisions of Article 120 of the Limitation Act, 1908, shall apply, not Article 44 of Schedule-1 of the Limitation Act, 1908. 

25. However, from the facts and circumstances proved in this case, as discussed herein before, I am of the opinion that, the plaintiff has not been able to prove any case of forgery of the disputed documents, as has been concurrently found by the courts below. Rather, the fact of guardianship being proved and admitted, in this case, Article 44 of Schedule-1of the Limitation Act, 1908, shall apply.

26. I have also considered the impugned judgment passed by the appellate court vis-à-vis the judgment of the trial court and the evidence on record. I find no case of misreading or non-reading of any evidence or misinterpretation of any law by the courts below. 

27. Before parting off, this Court should record that there are a good number of cases concerning the property and right of the minor's (who are indeed orphans). Hence, out of it's own anxiety to protect the rights and interest of the minors, this Court should pass necessary direction, to be effective prospectively.  (Emphasis added). 

28. Hence, in exercise of the powers vested in this Court under Article 112 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, the Inspector General of Registration (IGR) is hereby directed to prepare and publish a Circular or Office Order requiring all Sub-Registrars, in the case of registration of a deed as regards the property of a minor, who is represented by his or her guardian, to ensure that the deed of transfer or any other deed that purports to deal with the property of a minor contains within its recital the guardianship case number with the name of the concerned court and the permission case number with the name of the concerned court, with reference to which the executant claims to have derived authority to deal with the minor's property. 

29. The IGR shall send copies of the circular or office order, as the case may be, to the Secretary, Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs and to the Registrars of all Districts. 

30. The IGR should submit an affidavit of compliance to this Court within 45(forty five) working days from the date of receipt of this order through the Registrar, High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh. 

31. However, in view of the deliberation, recorded above, I am of the opinion that, this Rule has no merit and the same should be discharged. 

Order
In the result, the Rule is discharged. The impugned judgment and decree dated 10-4-2014 (decree signed on 15-4-2014), passed by the Joint District Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka, in Title Appeal No.135 of 2004, dismissing the appeal and thereby affirming the judgment and decree dated 10-4-2004 (decree signed on 17-4-2004), passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Savar, Dhaka, in Title Suit No.36 of 2002, is hereby upheld. 

The order of stay granted earlier by this Court is hereby vacated. 

No order as to cost. 

Let a copy of this judgment and order be sent to the Secretary, Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs, for information and record, so far the direction given in paragraph No. 29, herein above. 

Let a copy of this judgment and order be sent to the Inspector General of Registration (IGR), for necessary action and compliance, vide paragraph Nos. 27 to 30 herein above. 

Let another copy of this judgment and order be sent to the Registrar, High Court Division of the Supreme Court, so far as the question of compliance is concerned, vide paragraph Nos. 27 to 30, herein above. 

Let a copy of this judgment along with the Lower Court's Record be sent down to the concerned Courts, at once. 

End.
