parties:
Abu Nayem Bhuiyan (Md) and others --------- Petitioners
vs
Md Mosharaf Hossain and others -------- Opposite-Parties
full_judgment:
On an application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, this Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party Nos.1-3 to show cause as to why the judgment and order dated 23-8-2016 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Narayanganj in Miscellaneous Appeal No.10 of 2016 disallowing the same and thereby affirming the judgment and order dated 5-4-2016 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Narayanganj in Title Suit No.24 of 2016 rejecting the application for injunction should not be set-aside and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

2. Shorn of unnecessary details, fact of the case lies in a very short compus. The petitioners, as plaintiff, instituted Title Suit No.24 of 2016 in the Court of learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Narayanganj against the opposite-parties, as defendant on the following prayers; 
“(ক) বাদীগণ আরজির তফসিল বর্ণিত নালিশা সম্পত্তিতে ১৬ আনা স্বত্বে স্বত্ববান ও মালিক এবং ১-৩ নং বিবাদীগণ নালিশা সম্পত্তিতে অবৈধ দখলদার এই মর্মে বাদীগণের অনুকূল এবং ১-৩ নং বিবাদীগণের প্রতিকূল নালিশা সম্পত্তিতে বাদীগণের স্বত্ব ঘোষণা সহ এক খাস দখলের ডিক্রী দিতে এবং ১-৩ নং বিবাদীগণকে নালিশা সম্পত্তির দখল বাদীগণের বরাবর ফেরত প্রদানের জন্য এক সংর্কীণ সময় দিতে;
(খ) বিজ্ঞ আদালতের নির্ধারিত মেয়াদ মধ্যে ১-৩ নং বিবাদীগণ বাদীগণ বরাবর নালিশা সম্পত্তির দখল ফেরত না দিলে ১-৩ নং বিবাদীগণের যাবতীয় প্রতিবন্ধকতা রহিতে আদালতের মাধ্যমে বাদীগণকে নালিশা সম্পত্তির দখল পাইবার নির্দেশ দিতে;

3. Short facts of the case, are that the property in question was sold in auction for arrear rents in LR Sale Case No.1217 of 1952-53. One Abdul Latif Prodhan purchased the property in auction and got delivery of possession on 5-6-1955. Property under CS Khatian No.64 was in possession of one Bipin Behari Singh who refused to obtain settlement of the same on payment of rents to Abdul Latif Prodhan, consequently, the property was made khas by Abdul Latif Prodhan. In the way aforesaid Abdul Latif Prodhan while in possession and enjoyment of the property sold out a portion of the auction purchased property to the father of the plaintiff, Abul Khayrat Bhuiyan by a Registered Sale Deed No.4695 dated 22-6-1955. After death of Abul Khayrat Bhuiyan the plaintiffs as heirs acquired the property by inheritance and have been possessing the same in different ways by cultivating seasonal crops and rearing fishes in the low land. The defendants have had no title and possession in the property, but SA and RS khatians stood recorded in the name of vendors of the defendants who had no title and possession in the property. When the plaintiffs went to local Tahshil Office for payment of rents and mutation of their names, concerned officials refused to receive rent on the ground that khatian for the property stands in the name of defendant. Consequently, the plaintiff filed Title Suit No.332 of 2015 in the Court of Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Narayanganj for declaration of title and correction of the khatian against the government and others which is now pending for disposal. 

4. It is also stated that the property in question was declared by the government as vested and non resident property for which the plaintiffs filed Tribunal Suit No.6312 of 2013 seeking release of the property from the "Kha" list. Subsequently, the government by Gazette Notification dated 10-10-2013 excluded all the properties under "Kha" list, resultantly, the proceeding has become abated in favour of the plaintiff. Had there been any title and possession of the defendants in the suit property they would have filed case before the Tribunal for release of the property from the list of vested property. The defendants are mighty men and creating a sale deed from the SA and RS recordee forcibly entered into the property on 4-1-2016 and started cutting earth. The plaintiffs on coming to know hurriedly rushed to the suit property and prevented the defendants from cutting earth but the defendants by applying force continued to cut earth dispossessing the plaintiffs from the suit land denying title of the plaintiffs. The plaintiffs at the time of filing of the suit filed an application under Order 39 Rules 1 and 2 praying for injunction in the following terms; 

“যাবতীয় অবস্থা ও কারণাধীনে বাদীগণের বিনীত প্রার্থনা, অত্র মোকদ্দমা চলাকালে ১-৩ নং বিবাদীগণ যাহাতে নিম্ন তফসিল বর্ণিত নালিশা ভূমিতে কোনরূপ মাটি বা বালু ভরাট করিতে না পানে এবং নালিশা ভূমিতে কোন ড্রেজার স্থাপন করিতে না পারে এবং নালিশা সম্পত্তির আকৃতি ও প্রকৃতির পরিবর্তন ও পরিবর্ধন করিতে না পারে তন্যর্মে ১-৩নং বিবাদীগণের বিরুদ্ধে এক অস্থায়ী নিষেধাজ্ঞার আদেশ দানে
এবং
অস্থায়ী নিষেধাজ্ঞার দরখাস্ত নিষ্পত্তি না হওয়া পর্যন্ত ১-৩নং বিবাদীগণের বিরুদ্ধে উপরে বর্ণিত মতে এক অন্তবতীকালীন নিষেধাজ্ঞার আদেশ দানে বাধিত করিতে আজ্ঞা হয় ।”

5. The trial court on the very day of filing suit passed an order of status-quo on 10-1-2016 in the following terms; 

“ইতিমধ্যে অস্থায়ী নিষেধাজ্ঞার দরখাস্তের বিরুদ্ধে প্রতিপক্ষ/বিবাদী কর্তৃক আপত্তি দাখিল না করা পর্যস্ত নালিশি তপছিল বর্ণিত সম্পত্তিতে আকার/আকৃতি পরিবর্তন করিতে না পেরে তৎ্মর্মে উভয় পক্ষকে স্থিতাবস্থা বজায় রাখার নির্দেশ দেওয়া হইলে;”

6. Thereafter, the defendants appeared in suit and filed written objection against the prayer for injunction. The matter was hard by the trial court on 5-4-2016 and upon hearing by order dated 5-4-2016 injunction was refused. Thereafter, the plaintiffs preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No.10 of 2016 before the learned District Judge, Narayanganj which was subsequently, heard and disposed by the learned Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Narayanganj. On the very day of admitting appeal learned District Judge, Narayanganj passed an order on 6-6-2016 directing both the parties to maintain status-quo in respect of the suit property. The appellate court after haring appeal by the impugned judgment and order dated 23-8-2016 disallowed the appeal and vacated the order of status-quo. At this juncture, the petitioners moved this Court by filing this revisional application and obtained the present Rule and order of status-quo on 16-10-2016. 

7. The opposite-parties in their written objection against injunction application contended that the property originally belonged to Tarikanath Singh Roy and others. CS and SA khatian Nos.229 and 264 stood recorded in their names and RS Khatian also stood recorded in the names of some SA recordee and their heirs. The owners of the property while in possession and enjoyment by Deed No.7495 dated 8-9-1975 transferred the suit property to Amzad Hossain and 3(three) others and one Md Ramzan Ali purchaser of the property, by Deed No.1017 dated 6-2-2001 transferred the suit property to one Salema Begum and they got their names mutated in the khatian and paid rent to the government. They also claim that the plaintiff have no title and possession in the property for more than 60(sixty) years and did not pay any rent to the government and took no steps for correction of the khatian on the basis of purchase of their predecessor. The fact of dispossession by the defendants is false and fabricated. The plaintiffs never possessed the suit property but with the false allegation of dispossession filed the instant suit. 

8. Mr Md Imam Hossain, learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners submits that the property in question was put in auction in LR Sale Case No.1217 of 1952-53 which was purchased by one Abdul Latif Prodhan who got delivery of possession on 5-6-1955 and in support of such contention the plaintiffs could file some papers showing auction, Boinama and other connected papers. He further submits that the plaintiffs could file a Registered Deed No.4695 dated 22-6-1955 executed and registered by Abdul Latif Prodhan in favour of Abul Khayrat Bhuiyan, father of the plaintiffs and by the said deed vast property were transferred including the suit property. He further submits that except the suit plot other khatians for other property stood recorded in the name of the plaintiffs predecessor but inadvertently khatian for the suit property stood recorded in the name of the predecessor of the defendants for which another title suit is now pending. He further submits that in the instant suit a complicated question of title is involved and that can be determination at the time of hearing on evidences. But the defendants being mighty persons took possession of the property by dispossessing the plaintiffs and trying to construct structure thereon by changing the nature and character of the suit property which will lead further complication and create multiplicity of judicial proceedings. He finally submits that pending determination of the merit of the suit, to prevent abuse of the processes of law and to secure ends of justice, both the courts below as well as this Court at the time of filing of the suit, appeal and this revision granted an order of status-quo directing both the parties which is continuing till today. Candidly, he submits that for ends of justice and to prevent multiplicity of judicial proceedings this Rule may be disposed of maintaining order of status-quo granted at the time of issuance of the Rule directing the trial court to dispose of the suit within shortest possible time and in that situation parties to the proceedings will not be prejudice. 

9. Mr Kazi Mujibur Rahman, learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party Nos.1 and 3 submits that admittedly this is a suit for recovery of possession and declaration of title, meaning thereby, the plaintiffs are not in possession of the suit property. He further submits that except some papers relating to auction and sale deed of the year 1955, the plaintiffs could not produce any paper showing recording of their predecessor's name or their names in the khatian, payment of rent and even not a single evidence of possession, as such, plaintiffs out of possession not entitled to get injunction. He further submits that in the event of decreeing the suit in favour of the plaintiffs they will get possession of the property through court, as such, there is no earthly reason to prevent the defendants from developing the property by erecting structure or building thereon. He further submits that to get an order of injunction the plaintiffs must show a prima facie case, balance of convenience and inconveniences and irreparable loss, if the injunction is refused. But in the instant case the plaintiffs utterly failed to show a prima facie case in their favour and balance of convenience and inconveniences, as such, the Rule is liable to be discharged. 

10. Heard the learned Advocates of both the parties, have gone through the revisional application, plaint in suit, application for injunction, photocopies of papers and documents submitted by the petitioners by supplementary-affidavit and by the opposite-parties and the impugned judgment and order of both the courts below. 

11. From the statement made in the plaint as well as in the application for injunction, it appears that the property in question originally belonged to Tarikanath Singh Roy and 6(six) others as appearing from the khatian submitted by both the parties. The plaintiffs claim that the title of the CS recorded owner extinguish by auction sale in LR Sale Case No.1217 of 1952-53 and the property was purchased by one Abdul Latif Prodhan as appearing from Annexures-F series, annexed to the supplementary-affidavit filed by the petitioners. Said Abdul Latif Prodhan by a Sale Deed No.4695 dated 22-6-1955 transferred the suit property along with other properties to one Md Abul Khayrat Bhuiyan, father of the plaintiffs. Further it appears that SA and RS Khatians stand recorded in the name of the vendor of the defendants and the suit property in RS Khatian No.13 declared vested and non resident property. From Annexure-G1, annexed to the supplementary affidavit, it appears that the plaintiffs filed Tribunal Case No.63I2 of 2013 before the tribunal praying for release of the property from vested property list which was subsequently, abated and the property was released. 

12. On the other hand, the defendants by filing relevant CS, SA and RS khatians tried to show that the property belonged to Tarakanath Singh Roy and 6(six) others subsequently, owner of the property and their heirs transferred the property to the defendants in the year 1975. The plaintiffs claim that the Deed No.7495 dated 8-9-1975 is a forged and fabricated document. In the Registration Office no such sale deed was found allegedly have been executed by Asish Ranjan Singh Roy and 5(five) others in favour of Amzad Hossain and 2(two) others. 

13. Both the parties claim ownership of the property on the basis of purchase of the years 1955 and 1975. The suit now pending for disposal before the trial court, validity of the documents, claim and counter claim of the parties can only be determined by the trial court on evidence at the time of trial. But it is fact that the plaintiffs are not in possession of the suit property, however, their case is for recovery of possession on the ground of dispossession and the matter of dispossession or possession is a matter to be decided on evidences. 

14. Apparently, the plaintiffs claim title in the property on the basis of auction and purchase of their father from the auction purchaser in the year 1955 and the defendants claim the property on the basis of record of right and by purchase in the year 1975. Here a complicated question of title is involved in the present suit but it appears that the trial court at the first instance passed an order of status-quo and it was continued upto disposal of the injunction matter. Thereafter, the appellate court also passed an order of status-quo which was continued till disposal of the appeal and this Court also at the time of issuance of Rule passed an order of status-quo which is still subsisting. Since a complicated question of title is involved in the instant suit along with possession and dispossession, this Court thinks that the purpose of the parties will be served and justice would be done if the Rule is disposed of maintaining the order of status-quo granted by this Court at the time of issuance of the Rule to secure ends of justice and to prevent further multiplicity of judicial proceedings, directing the trial court to dispose of the suit within a shortest possible time giving top most priority. 

15. In view of the above, this Court refrains itself from entering into the merit of the case and inclined to maintain the order of status-quo passed at the time of issuance of the Rule, directing the trial court to dispose of the suit on an urgent basis. 

16. In the result, the Rule is disposed of, however, without any order as to costs. 

17. Both the parties are hereby directed to maintain status-quo in respect of nature and character of the suit property till disposal of the suit. 

18. The trial court is hereby directed to dispose of Title Suit No.24 of 2016 as well as Title Suit No.332 of 2015 within a shortest possible time preferable within 6(six) months from the date of receipt of this judgment giving top most priority. 

Communicate a copy of the judgment to the Court concerned at once. 

End.

lawyer:
Md Saiful Islam, Advocate—For the Petitioner.

Samarendra Nath Biswas, DAG with Md Abul Kalam Khan Daud, AAG with AHM Ziauddin, AAG with Md Modersher Ali Khan (Dipu), AAG with Rehana Sultana, AAG—For the Respondents-Government.
parties:
Mohammad Ullah Mintu and another ------- Petitioner
vs
Commissioner of Customs, Customs House, Chattogram and others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
SM Maniruzzaman, J: In this Rule Nisi, issued under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, the respondents have been called upon to show cause as to why failure of the respondents to make final assessment of the petitioner's imported goods covered under Letter of Credit No. 00000-296816010696 dated 27-10-2016 under Bill of Entry No. C-150121 dated 31-1-2017 within the stipulated period of 120 (one hundred and twenty) working days from the date of provisional assessment under the provision of section 81(2) of the Customs Act, 1969 should not be declared to have been done without lawful authority and hence, of no legal effect and also as to why a direction shall not be given upon the respondents to release/return the bank guarantee being No. SJIBL/BANG/ INV /BG-01 /2017 dated 15-2-2017 for Taka 26,96,001.89 (Taka twenty six lac ninety six thousand one and paisa eighty nine) lying with the respondent No. 4 and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

2. However, at the time of issuance of the Rule, the contending parties were directed to maintain status-quo in respect of encashment of the bank guarantee for a prescribed period.

3. Facts, relevant for disposal of the Rule, in short, are that the petitioner is proprietor of "M/s BM International" and is engaged in the business of import various commodity from abroad and after importation sells the same in the local market. 

4. In course of his business, he opened Letter of Credit No. 00000-296816010696 dated 27-10-2016 for importing "Seamless Pipe ASTM" from China under HS Code No. 7304.23.20. After arrival of the goods at Chattogram port, the petitioner however, collected shipping documents from his bank and accordingly, submitted the same to the customs authority through his C&F Agent for assessment and releasing the goods. After submitting the shipping documents, the customs authority generated Bill of Entry being No. C-150121 dated 31-1-2017 for assessment and releasing of the goods. Thereafter, the concerned respondent customs authority physically examined the goods and did not accept the HS Code of the goods as declared by the petitioner. Rather, determined the goods to fall under. HS Code No. 7304.90.00. The customs authority also suggested that the goods required to be (sample) examined in the BUET for determining the correct applicable HS Code. In this regard, the authority concerned suggested to allow the petitioner to release the goods by provisional assessment on furnishing bank guarantee for the differential amount of duty and taxes between the declared HS Code No. 7304.23.20 and the proposed HS Code No. 7304.90.00. 

5. The petitioner duly accepted the said proposal of the respondent customs authority and made payment of all customs duties and taxes as his declared HS Code in cash and furnished bank guarantee being No. SJIBL/ BANG /INV/BG-01/2017 dated 15-2-2017 for Taka 26,96,001.89 (Taka twenty six lac ninety six thousand one and paisa eighty nine) for the differential amount of duty and taxes. Pursuant thereto the customs authority released 'the goods on provisional assessment dated 19-2-2017. 

6. However, the categorical assertion of the petitioner is that after releasing the respective goods by provisional assessment, the concerned respondent customs authority did not complete final assessment as required under section 81(2) of the Act, 1969. After expiry of the statutory period of 120 working days the respondent No. 2 asked the petitioner through his C&F Agent to deposit required amount of money for chemical examination of the goods in order to determine the correct HS Code for the purpose of final assessment of the imported goods. 

7. It has been stated further that the goods in question has been released by the petitioner of an provisional assessment dated 19-2-2017 and the concerned respondent failed to complete final assessment within the said statutory period of 120 working days. The petitioner challenging the in action of the respondent to release the bank guarantee due to failure final assessment within time filed writ petition No. 18820 of 2017 and accordingly, Rule Nisi was issued and also was given direction upon the respondent concern to dispose of the representation filed by the petitioner dated 14-12-2017 in respect of releasing the bank guarantee. Accordingly, the respondent customs authority disposed of the representation dated 14-12-2017 vide the order dated 29-10-2018 refusing to release the bank guarantee in favour of the petitioner. The said Rule was discharged for non prosecution vide order dated 12-5-2019. 

8. By the supplementary-affidavit it has been stated further that the petitioner after discharging the Rule of writ petition No. 18820 of 2017 filed a representation dated 7-7-2019 to the respondent No. 1 for releasing the bank guarantee but, the respondent did not response therein till date.

9. In that view of the matter, the petitioner has filed the instant writ petition challenging the inaction of the respondents failure to make final assessment of his imported goods within due time as required under the law and also seeking direction to return the bank guarantees furnished by hint before the respondent customs authority as security on provisionally assessment and accordingly, obtained the present Rules along with order of status quo. 

10. Mr Md Saiful Islam, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner of all the writ petitions submits that the respondent customs authority miserably failed to make final assessment of the imported goods of the petitioner as per the specific provision of law, in as much as, section 81 of the Act, 1969 clearly stipulates to make final assessment of goods within 120 (one hundred and twenty) working days from the date of provisional assessment and the concerned respondents failed to make final assessment of the imported goods of the petitioner within the said stipulated period; and thus, acted illegally. He lastly goes to argue that the date of provisional assessment of the goods in question on 19-2-2017 and the concerned respondents failed to make provisional assessment of the petitioner's imported goods final within of the said statutory period 120 (one twenty) working days under section 81(2) of the Act, 1969, which is a mandatory provision of law but grossly violated by the remiss actions of the respondents and for these bank guarantees furnished by the petitioner in good faith are now at risk of sudden arbitrally encashment by the respondents. Accordingly, he submits that a direction is required to be given upon the respondent No. 1 to return/release the bank guarantee being No. SJIBL/BANG/INV/BG-01/2017 dated 15-2-2017 issued by Shahjalal Islami Bank Ltd, Bangshal Branch, Dhaka lying with them in favour of the petitioner. In support of his aforesaid submissions, the learned Advocate for the petitioner has referred to the decisions of the case of Government of Bangladesh and others vs Md Salim Hossain reported in 11 BLT (AD) page 71 and Nasir Glass Industries Limited vs National Board of Revenue and others reported in 17 BLT (HCD) 243. 

11. Per contra, Mr Abdul Kalam Khan Daud, the learned Assistant Attorney-General entered appearance on behalf of the respondent No. 1, Commissioner of Customs by filing Vokalatnama. No affidavit in opposition has been filed by the concerned respondent controverting the assertions so made in the writ petition. So, the statement made in the writ petition has been uncontroverted. However, the learned Assistant Attorney-General submits that the goods has been released by the customs authority on provisional assessment as the instance of petitioner but, the petitioner however did not deposit expenses for chemical examination of the goods as required under section 200 of the Act till date and for this reason, the respondent customs authority could not complete chemical examination of the goods in question. Hence, the petitioner cannot claim any benefit for his own fault. 

12. In the said context the learned Assistant Attorney-General prays that the Rule may be disposed of with direction upon the respondent concern to complete final assessment of the goods in question as early as possible. 

13. Heard the learned Advocate for the petitioner of all the writ petitions and the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the respondent No. 1, have perused the writ petitions, materials on record so appended thereto and relevant provision of law. 

14. The cardinal issue requires to be determined in this writ petitions is that whether the customs authorities have completed final assessment of the petitioner's imported goods in question within the stipulated period of 120 working days as prescribed under section 81 of the Act, 1969 and the petitioner is entitled to get return the bank guarantees furnished by him at the time of releasing of the goods on provisional assessment. 

15. In order to appreciate the respective arguments of both the parties, it is pertinent to look into the relevant provision of law i.e. section 81 of the Act, 1969 for proper disposal of the instant Rules. Section 81 reads as follows; 
81. Provisional assessment of duty.—(1) Where it is not possible immediately to assess the customs duty that may be payable on any imported goods entered for home-consumption of for warehousing or for clearance from a warehouse for home-consumption or on any goods entered for exportation, for the reason that the goods require chemical or other test [or a further enquiry] for purposes of assessment, or that all the documents or complete documents or full information pertaining to those goods have not been furnished, an officer not below that rank of [Assistant Commissioner of Customs] may order that the duty payable on such goods be assessed provisionally: 
Provided that the importer (same in the case of goods entered for warehousing) or the exporter pays such additional amount as security or furnishes such guarantee of a scheduled bank for the payment thereof as the said officer deems sufficient to meet the excess of the final assessment of duty over the provisional assessment. [(2) Where any goods are allowed to be cleared or delivered on the basis of such provisional assessment, the amount of duty actually payable on those goods shall, within a period of one hundred and twenty working days from the date of the provisional assessment, where there is a case pending at any court, tribunal or appellate authority, from the date of receipt of the final disposal order of that case, be finally assessed and on completion of such assessment the appropriate officer shall order that the amount already guaranteed be adjusted against the amount payable on the basis of final assessment, and the difference between them shall be paid forthwith to or by the importer or exporter as the case may be: 
Provided that the Board may, under exceptional circumstances recorded in writing, extend the period of final assessment specified under this sub-section. 

16. Section 81 provides that when the customs authority is of the opinion that it is not possible to assess the duty and taxes immediately that may be payble on any imported goods or any goods entered for exportation for the reason that the goods require chemical or other test for purpose of assessment or that all the documents or complete documents or full information pertaining to those goods have not been furnished, an officer not below the rank of Assistant Commissioner of Customs may order that the duty payable on such goods be assessed provisionally. The importer or exporter pays such additional amount as security or furnishes such guarantee of a schedule bank for the payment thereof as the officer seems sufficient to meet the excess of the final assessment of duty over the provisional assessment. When any goods are released on the basis of such provisionally assessment, the amount of duty actually payable on those goods shall, within a period of 120 (one hundred twenty) working days be finally assessed but where any case pending before the any Court, or authority the date for final assessment be counted from the date of receipt of the final disposal order of the case. As per proviso of this section only the Board may under exceptional circumstances recorded in writing extend the period of final assessment specified under this section.

17. In the instance case admittedly the petitioner released his imported goods on provisional assessment dated 19-2-2017 on furnishing bank guarantee for the differential amount of duties and taxes as security. 

18. However, the concerned customs authorities failed to complete provisional assessment as final within the prescribed period of 120 working days and also failed to extend the said period for final assessment from the Board as per proviso of section 81(2) of the Act, 1969; although, they could have assessed the goods finally under the said provision of law, but they did not take any step to that effect as yet. It appears from the record that 208 days was expired from the date of provisional assessment till the date on 21-12-2017 i.e. till filing of writ petition No. 18820 of 2017. 

19. In this regard in the case of Government of Bangladesh and others vs Md Salim Hossain (Supra), it has been held that; 
"The customs authority as per provision of section 81 of the Act was required to make the provisional assessment final within the reasonable time. In respect of the consignments of the respondent the customs authority made provisional assessment in between July, 1991 and February, 1992, but till August 1997 the customs authority did not make the assessment final although the authority had the materials before it for making the final assessment of duties and other levies on the imported goods of the respondent taking the value at US$ 400 per Metric ton. The customs authority inspire of having the materials for making the provisional assessment final did not make final assessment till August, 1997 taking the value of the imported goods at US$ 400 per Metric ton. The customs authority inspire of having the materials for making the provisional assessment final did not make final assessment till August, 1997 taking the value of the imported goods at US$ 400 per metric ton, and thus the respondent was compelled to file the writ petitions seeking direction for the refund of the excess amount of duties realized from him at the time of provisional assessment without legal basis. In our view in the background of the facts of the case the High Court Division has committed no error in making direction for refund of the excess amount of duties realized against the goods imported by the respondent" 

20. Similar view has been adopted by this High Court Division in the case of Nasir Glass Industries Limited vs National Board of Revenue and others (Supra) that; "Section 81(2) of the Customs Act categorically says that the final assessment is to be made within 150 working days from the date of release of the goods on the basis of provisional assessment and since more than 180 days have passed after provisional assessment made on 17-5-2005, the Customs authority under no circumstances can ask for encashment of the bank guarantee. Thus, since the respondents failed to obtain an expert opinion and since the respondents failed to assess the goods finally within 150 working days from the date of provisional assessment the order for encashment of the bank guarantee by the impugned letter is illegal and without lawful authority." 

21. In view of the statutory provision of law and the ratio settled by our Apex Court, we are of the view that on the failure of the customs authority to complete provisional assessment as final within the statutory period of 120 working days as prescribed under section 81(2) of the Act, 1969 or failure to extend the said period for final assessment from the Board, the provisional assessment made by the customs authority on the basis of declared value/H.S. Code shall be deemed to be treated as final. Consequent thereof the concerned importer/ exporter is entitled to get return the bank guarantee(s) furnished by him as security on provisional assessment. 

22. In the instant case admittedly, the respondents customs authorities failed to assess the goods in question finally within the said statuary period; moreso, it also failed to show from record that said period has subsequently be extended by the Board in exercise of power as provided under the proviso to sub-section (2) of section 81 of the Act. In view of the above stated position of fact the customs authority has no scope to withheld the bank guarantee furnished by the petitioner for the differential amount of duties and taxes against the provisional assessment of the imported goods in question as security for the purpose of final assessment. 

23. In view of the above facts and circumstances of the cases, findings and observations we find substance in the submissions made by the learned Advocate for the petitioner and merit of the Rule. 

24. Accordingly, the Rule is made absolute. 

25. The respondent No. 1, the Commissioner of Customs, Customs House, Chattogram is directed to return the bank guarantee No. SJIBL/BANG/INV/BG-01/2017 dated 15-2-2017 issued by the Shahjalal Islami Bank Ltd, Bangshal Branch, Dhaka in favour of the petitioner within 30 days from the date of receipt of the copy of this judgment and order positively. 

26. There will be no order as to costs.
 
27. The order of status quo granted earlier by this Court is hereby recalled and vacated. 

Communicate the copy of this judgment and order to the concerned respondents forthwith. 

End.

Nasima K. Hakim, DAG with Tahmina Polly, AAG, Elin Saha, AAG and Ziaul Hakim, AAG—For the Respondents.

full_judgment:
Syed Refaat Ahmed, J: In this Application under Article 102(2) of the Constitution a Rule Nisi was issued on 1-7-2019 calling upon the Respondents to show cause as to why purported action of the Respondent No. 2 to shut down the ASYCUDA World System on 12-6-2019 from 3-53 pm for generating Bill of Entry registration on 12-6-2019 as contained in ANNEXURE-E, E-1 and E-2 in violation of its notice No. নথি নং এস-২৩/আমদানী-(০৯ অংশ ৪) dated 11-6-2019 as contained in ANNEXURE-F should not be declared unlawful, illegal, without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and as to why the Respondent No. 2 should not be directed to generate the Bill of Entry in accordance with the notice No. নথি নং এস-২৩/আমদানী-(০৯ অংশ ৪) dated 11-6-2019 as contained in ANNEXURE-F and generate the Bill of Entry on the customs duty prevailing on 12-6-2019 and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

2. The proper and accurate operation and administration of the Automated System for Customs Data ("ASYCUDA") computerized system goes to the root of this case. ASYCUDA was designed by the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) to administer a country's customs and constitutes the UNCTAD's largest technical cooperation programme spanning over 80 countries and regional projects including Bangladesh. UNCTAD'S aim is to aid customs authorities worldwide to automate and control their core processes and obtain timely, accurate and relevant information to facilitate government policy projections and planning. Of the three generations of. ASYCUDA in use, ASYCUDA World in the most recent and is presently in use in Bangladesh. The ASYCUDA World System is web-based thus allowing users to access it and process transactions from any location at any point in time especially to submit commercial documents electronically. Conceived as an integrated customs management tool for international trade and transport operations in a state-of-the-art automated environment, the core objective of this system is to both increase the effective collection of customs revenues and strengthen institutional mechanisms for customs data collection and processing contributing effectively to increased revenue earnings from trade. 

3. The Petitioner operates in the private sugar industry sector by importing raw cane sugar and refining it for local consumption. In the course of one such importation the Petitioner submitted the relevant Import General Manifest (IGM) on 12-6-2019 but due to a shutdown of the ASYCUDA World System at Chittagong Port, the Petitioner was prevented in the facts from submitting the relevant Bill of Entry for unloading its imported consignment of Brazilian raw cane sugar. 

4. It. is in the regular course of the operation of its industry that the Petitioner imported 54,000 MT raw cane sugar in bulk from Brazil as carried on board by the vessel MV Heilan Brother that left the port in Brazil on 11-5-2019 and reached anchorage of Chittagong Port on 12-6-2019 at 12-00 pm. 

5. A chronological breakdown of the events unfolding thereafter is crucial to a proper understanding of the Petitioner's case. To begin with on 12-6-2019 at 2-24 pm the master of MV Heilan Brother served the Notice of Readiness ("NoR") to the Petitioner and the port authority followed by the submission of the IGM in the ASYCUDA World System being No. 2019/2104 at 3-53 pm. Thereafter, the Petitioner at 4-04 pm, 4-11 pm and 4-16 pm successively tried to upload the Bill of Entry into the system but the system was shut down and the Bill of Entry registration was not resumed until 5-00 pm the next day on 13-6-2019 resulting in a delayed registration as had significant substantive and financial consequences for the Petitioner much to its chagrin. 

6. It had so come to pass that the Respondent No. 2, Commissioner of Customs, Customs House, Chittagong had issued a notice being No. নথি নং এস-২৩/আমদানী-(০৯ অংশ ৪) the previous day on 11-6-2019 as circulated among concerned C&F agents putting all on notice of the shutting down of the ASYCUDA World System on the terms, “বাজেট ঘোষণার দিন অর্থাৎ ১৩-৬-২০১৯ খ্রি: তারিখে রাত ১১টা হতে ১৪-৬-২০১৯ খ্রি: তারিখ রাত ৯-০০টা পর্যন্ত অনলাইনের Bill of Entry (BE) দাখিলের কার্যক্রম বন্ধ থাকিবে।, i.e., Online submission of Bill of Entry to remain suspended from 11-00 pm, 13-6-2019 to 9-00 pm, 14-6-2019 on account of the Budget being announced on 13-6-2019. 

7. It so transpired that on 13-6-2019, the government announced its annual budget and proposed to increase existing specific duty on sugar on the following terms "Sugar: I propose to increase existing specific duty from Taka 2000/MT to Taka 3000/MT on import of raw sugar. For refined sugar the specific duty will be increased from Taka 4,500 /MT to Taka 6,000/MT. Regulatory duty will be 30% instead of 20% for both refined and raw sugar import". 

8. In stark contrast to the terms of the notice of 11-6-2019, the Respondent No. 2, Commissioner of Customs, Customs House, Chittagong shut down the ASYCUDA World System throughout the day on 13-6-2019, and the next two dates, i.e., 14-6-2019 and 15-6-2019 constituting the two-day Friday and Saturday weekend in Bangladesh the Petitioner was, therefore, unable to generate its Bill of Entry duly. Furthermore, when finally the Petitioner on 16-6-2019 tried to secure a Bill of Entry registration the server would not permit it to generate such registration on the basis of customs duty prevailing on 12-6-2019. It is now the Petitioner's contention that the Respondent No. 2 had contrived to most illegally shut down the ASYCUDA World System in violation of the notice of 11-6-2019, thereby, preventing the Petitioner to duly generate its Bill of Entry registration at the rate of customs duty prevailing on 12-6-2019. Further the vessel MV Heilan Brother having berthed on 12-6-2019 and the Bill of Entry being presented on 12-6-2019 it is contended that the importation was completed well before 13-6-2019 and the Petitioner is entitled to be charged customs duty at the rate current on 12-6-2019. The cumulative effect of such entitlement, it is submitted, is that the Petitioner has acquired a vested right to get the consignment cleared at the rate of customs duty prevalent and current on 12-6-2019. The Respondents having shut down the said system long before than the time stipulated in the notice dated 11-6-2019, they, are viewed by the Petitioner as most illegally having prevented the Petitioner from submitting the Bill of Entry from 4-04 pm onwards on 12-6-2019. 

9. The issue focal to the Petitioner's case is that it could not and was not able to generate the Bill of Entry registration at the rate of Customs Duty prevailing on 12-6-2019 purely on account of a systemic error and contingency amounting to a fault attributable to the Respondents. It is the Petitioner's case that this is a contingency or an occurrence that was not contemplated or anticipated in the notice of 11-6-2019 and indeed is an issue that the Respondents have not addressed at all in responding to the Rule Nisi. 

10. The points made by the Respondents to counter the Petitioner's arguments are whittled down to the following: 
a) In accordance with section 43 of the Customs Act, 1969 ("Act"), the master of the vessel ought to have submitted the IGM before Customs officers or any other person authorized to receive the same. 
b) The Petitioner's authorized agent GM Shipping electronically transmitted the IGM from the ASYCUDA World System on 12-6-2019 at 3-53 pm but failed to obtain a counter-signature of the Customs Authority under section 46 of the Act and that failing such counter-signature no registration of the IGM can be deemed to have taken place to the complete satisfaction of the concerned superintendent of Customs until 2-18 pm on 17-6-2019. 
c) ASYCUDA World System is maintained centrally by the National Board of Revenue ("NBR"). As per the notice dated 11-6-2019 the ASYCUDA World System was shut down automatically from 13-6-2019 at 11-00 pm and from 15-6-2019 the system was open for Bill of Entry registration. 
d) Money Bill 2019 was placed in Parliament on 13-6-2019 amending the rate of customs duties, taxes and other charges. As per section 30 of the Act and the Provisional Collection of Taxes Act, 1931, it is clear that when the Budget is pronounced, the duty/taxes as fixed in the Money Bill shall be the basis for assessment. 

11. The sum total of the Respondents' assertions above is that the Petitioner failed to submit its Bill of Entry before 13-6-2019 and must now be subject to the new rates leviable under the Budget announced on and effective from that date onwards. 

12. It is evident to this Court upon a perusal of the pleadings and upon a consideration of the submissions placed before it that the Petitioner's consignment of Brazilian raw cane sugar entered Bangladesh on 12-6-2019 and that the vessel MV Heilan Brother was berthed at 12-30 pm on 12-6-2019, thereby, leading to our preliminary finding that the importation occurred well before 13-6-2019. It is also evident from documents brought on record that the relevant Bill of Entry was presented on 12-6-2019 but it is only by reason of unforeseeable circumstances brought on by a server failure that the Petitioner could not obtain the Bill of Entry registration. 

13. It is at this juncture that this Court deems it pertinent to reproduce the above mentioned notice dated 11-6-2019 as found annexed as Annexure-'F' in its entirety (the original notice being produced in an illegible form this reproduction is drawn from a typed version of the same produced by the Petitioner replete, however, with typographical errors and all effort has been made to remedy and correct the same in the text provided below):

গণপ্রজাতন্ত্রী বাংলাদেশ সরকার
কাস্টম হাউজ, চট্টগ্রাম ।
বিজ্ঞপ্তি

নথি নং এস-২৩/আমদানী-(০৯ অংশ ৪)
তারিখ:- ১১-৬-২০১৯ খ্রিঃ
বিষয়ঃ প্রাক বাজেট সতর্কতামূলক ব্যবস্থা গ্রহণ ।

(১) এতদ্বারা সংশ্লিষ্ট সকলের অবগতির জন্য জানানো যাচ্ছে যে, আগামী ১৩-৬-২০১৯ খ্রিঃ তারিখে ২০১৯-২০২০ অর্থবছরের বাজেট ঘোষণা হতে যাচ্ছে। পূর্বের ন্যায় এবারের বাজেটেও আমদানীকৃত পণ্যের শুক্কহারের ক্ষেত্রে পরিবর্তনের সম্ভাবনা থাকায় সতর্ক মূলক ব্যবস্থা হিসেবে নিম্নবর্ণিত কার্যক্রম গ্রহণের জন্য নির্দেশনা প্রদান করা হলোঃ
(ক) আগামী ১১-৬-২০১৯ খ্রিঃ তারিখ হতে ১৩-৬-২০১৯ খ্রিঃ তারিখ পর্যন্ত পণ্যবাহী জাহাজের বন্দরে আগমন নিশ্চিত হওয়া সাপেক্ষে অনলাইনে দাখিলকৃত IGM এর রেজিস্ট্রেশন প্রদান করা হবে। IGM শাখার দায়িত্প্রাপ্ত অফিস সুপার/কম্পিউটার অপারেটর কোন জাহাজের বিপরীতে দাখিলকৃত মেনিফেস্টর রেজিস্ট্রেশন প্রদানের পূর্বে এঁ জাহাজ বাংলাদেশের জলসীমায় প্রবেশ করেছে কিনা তা নিশ্চিত হয়ে IGM শাখায় দায়িতৃপ্রাপ্ত ডেপুটি কমিশনারের অনুমোদন সাপেক্ষে রেজিস্ট্রেশন প্রদান করবেন ।
(গ) ইতোমধ্যে যে সকল IGM এর রেজিস্ট্রেশন প্রদান করা হয়েছে যে সকল IGM এর ক্ষেত্রে জাহাজ বন্দরে আগমন নিশ্চিত হওয়া সাপেক্ষে Bill of Entry দাখিলের অনুমতি প্রদান করা হয়। পূর্বে রেজিস্ট্রেশন নম্বর বন্দরকৃত জাহাজের আগমন বিলম্বের ক্ষেত্রে IGM শাখার দায়িত্প্রাপ্ত ডেপুটি ফমিশনার সংশ্লিষ্ট Bill of Entry সমূহ ব্লক করে রাখবেন । পরবর্তীকালে জাহাজ বন্দরে আগমন নিশ্চিত হওয়া সাপেক্ষে IGM, Bill of Entry সমূহ আনলক করে IGM, Bill of Lading Rea Gar Sarge করবেন।
(গ) বাজেট ঘোষণার দিন অর্থাৎ ১৩-৬-২০১৯ খ্রিঃ তারিখে রাত ১১ টা হতে ১৪-৬-২০১৯ খ্রিঃ তারিখ রাত ৯-০০ টা পর্যস্ত অনলাইনে Bill of Entry (BE) দাখিলের কার্যক্রম বন্ধ থাকিবে । সিস্টেম ম্যামেরা, রাজস্ব বোর্ড, সেগুন বাগিচা, ঢাকা বিষয়টি নিশ্চিত করবেন ।
(ঘ) ঘোষিত বাজেটে যে সকল পণ্যের ক্ষেত্রে HS Code (Cardiff Line) প্রযোজ্য এর বিপরীতে শুক্ষ/কর পরিবর্তন হ্রাস/বৃদ্ধি করা হবে । সে সকল ক্ষেত্রে বাজেট ঘোষণার দিন হতে ৩০-৬-২০১৯ খ্রিঃ তারিখ পর্যন্ত দাখিলকৃত Bill of Entry (BE)  সামরিক শুক্কায়ন করতে হবে এবং শুল্কায়িত Bill of Entry (BE) “সাময়িক শুল্কায়িত” মর্মে সীল প্রদান করতে হবে। এছাড়া সংশ্লিষ্ট বিল অব এন্ট্রির Inspection Act-এ সাময়িক শুল্কায়নের বিষয়টি লিপিবদ্ধ রাখতে হবে ৷ অতঃপর বাজেট চূড়ান্ত ভাবে অনুমোদনের পর চূড়ান্ত শুল্কায়ন করতে হবে ।
(ঙ) শুন্তহারের পরিবর্তন (যদি থাকে) গ্যাসাইকুডা ওয়ার্ড সিস্টেম আপডেট না হওয়া পর্স্ত বাজেট ঘোষণার দিন হতে পরে দাখিলকৃত কোন শুক্কায়ন করা যাবে না। শুন্কহারের পরিবর্তন (যদি থাকে) ASYCUDA World System বা আপডেট না হওয়া পর্যন্ত বাজেট দলিলাদির মুদ্রিত কপি দেখে শুন্কহার সম্পর্কে নিশ্চিত হয়ে এসিস্ট্যান্ট কমিশনার অব কাস্টমস এর নিঙ্নে নয়, এমন কর্মকর্তা পর্যায়ে শুল্কায়ন করতে হবে । প্রয়োজনে আইন অনুযায়ী সরকারের রাজস্ব সুরক্ষা হয় এমন ব্যবস্থা এ্রহণ সাপেক্ষে সাময়িক শুস্কায়ন করতে হবে।
চে) কোন IGM সংশ্লিষ্ট Bill of Entry এর বিপরীতে বাজেট ঘোষণার তারিখের পূর্বে দাখিলকৃত Bill of Entry (BE) যেন পুনরায় দাখিল করা না হয় তা এ্যাসাইকুডা ওয়ার্ড সিস্টেম এ নিশ্চিত করতে হবে। গ্যাসাইকুডা ওয়ার্ড টীম এবং কাস্টম হাউজ, চট্টগ্রামের অপারেশন ফ্যানেজার এ বিষয়ে ব্যবস্থা নিবেন।
ছে) এস আর ও নং- ৩৩১ আইন/২০১৬/৬৭/কাস্টমস তারিখ ১-১১-২০১৬ খ্রিঃ এর যেসব HC Code এর বিপরীতে Minimum value রয়েছে সেসব পণ্যের শুল্কায়ন ক্ষেত্রে বিশেষ সাবধানতা অবলম্বন করতে হবে ।
(ক্র) আগামী ১৪-৬-২০১৯ খ্রিঃ তারিখ সকাল ৯.৩০ সংক্রান্ত আদেশ নির্দেশ নিয়ে একটি বাজেট পর্যালোচনা সভা অনুষ্ঠিত হবে । উক্ত সভায় সহকারী রাজস্ব কর্মকর্তাসহ তদুর্ সকল কর্মকর্তাগণ তাদের মতাম্তসহ উপস্থিত থাকবেন ।
(২) এ আদেশ জনস্বার্থে জারী করা হলো ।”

14. Upon a first reading of the notice, and in particular clause 1(ক) of the notice, it is noted that the notice in recognition of the overriding public interest intended to be served by its issuance in clause 1(ক) expressly and categorically states that the ASYCUDA World System বাজেট ঘোষণার দিন অর্থাৎ ১৩-৬-২০১৯ খ্রিঃ তারিখে রাত ১১টা হতে ১৪-৬-২০১৯খ্রিঃ তারিখ রাত ৯-০০টা পর্যন্ত অনলাইনে Bill of Entry (BE) দাখিলের কার্যক্রম বন্ধ থাকিবে। But, and as indeed acknowledged by the Respondents themselves, the said system became inoperative or was shutdown long before the designated date and time, thereby, preventing and impairing an importer like the Petitioner from submitting the Bill of Entry despite several attempts made from 4-04 pm on 12-6-2019. 

15. The Affidavit-in-Opposition upon a first reading strikes this Court as being an exercise in obfuscating the primary responsibility that ought to have been assumed by the Respondents for an otherwise admitted and acknowledged systemic error that has given rise to a substantive legal issue for consideration by this Court. Indeed it is this Court's view that the systemic error with which the Petitioner was faced on 12-6-2019 wholly set at naught the otherwise carefully crafted mechanism for assessment evident in the notice read by this Court as issued under section 219B of the Act on 11-6-2019. The Respondents furthermore, have tried to evade responsibility for such wrongdoing before this Court in a manner in which the possibility of mala fide in engineering such a system error or fault cannot wholly be ruled out. The systemic error has occurred in the facts in a manner that is, therefore, wholly opaque as the Respondents seem highly reluctant to discharge their onus of explaining why and how such an error arose in a manner as the Petitioner contends has adversely affected its vested right for its goods to be assessed at the rate of duty as prevailed on 12-6-2019 and as indeed contemplated in the law under section 30 of the Act. 

16. The Affidavit-in-Opposition of the Respondent No. 2 Commissioner of Customs, Customs House, Chittagong reflects to this Court a conscious exercise to avoid addressing the reason behind and the substantive fallout of the otherwise tacitly acknowledged fact of systemic error having occurred on 12-6-2019. As part of that exercise, for example, there is no meaningful attempt by the Respondent No. 2 to address the reality of the situation as clearly recorded in all relevant documents. The effort instead is to rely on misconceived readings of the law and accord such provisions an interpretation that defies all sense and reason. Take for example, therefore, the acknowledgment by the Respondent No. 2 that the authorized agent of the Petitioner did indeed electronically transmit the IGM from the ASYCUDA World System on 12-6-2019 at 3-53 pm "but have failed to take counter signed (sic) by the Customs Authority under Section 46 of the Customs Act, 1969". To take this erroneous point further, and without any substantiation of any kind, the Respondent No. 2, Commissioner carries on further by contending that-
"unless countersigned by the customs authority under section 46 of the Customs Act, it cannot be termed as registered IGM and thereupon after complete satisfaction of the concerned superintendent of Customs, the agent of the Petitioner obtained IGM from the ASYCUDA World System on 17-6-2019 at 2-18 pm" 

17. It is here at this juncture that the learned Advocate for the Petitioner Mr Kamal-ul Alam has intervened, and aptly so, to draw attention to section 46 of the Act as deals with the duty of the person receiving an import manifest by categorically laying down inter alia: 
"and where the import manifest is transmitted electronically to the Customs computer system by a registered user, the import manifest shall be deemed to have been countersigned by the person authorized to receive such transmission and that person shall comply with the direction of that Commissioner, if any, in this regard." 

18. It is this Court's finding that this rebuttal by Mr Kamal-ul Alam by reference to this deeming provision in section 46 of the Act completely diminishes the effect of the Respondent No. 2, Commissioner's contention that the lack of counter-signature in the circumstances proved fatal for the Petitioner and indeed the merit of this case bearing in mind further that the Respondent No. 2, Commissioner through his pleadings and the learned Deputy Attorney General, Ms. Nasima K. Hakim in her submissions have never questioned the authenticity of the documents relied upon by the Petitioner and the veracity of the contents of such documents. 

19. It is at this juncture that this Court addresses the legal submissions placed by Mr Kamal-ul Alam purely by reference to the law to substantiate the Petitioner's case before us. Before embarking on that exercise this Court is, however, obliged to address the matter of the maintainability of this Writ Petition as raised by the Respondent No. 2, Commissioner and agitated to some extent by the learned DAG consequentially. This bears reference to an earlier Writ Petition being No. 6713 of 2019 filed by the Petitioner as may have had touched upon facts and issues as arise in this case. The learned DAG up to a certain point appeared to have hinted at the pendency still of Writ Petition No. 6713 of 2019 and, thereby, appeared keen on raising the spectre of res judicata in this case. Those concerns of the Respondents have been laid to rest, however, by a system check conducted by this Court as reveals that Writ Petition No. 6713 of 2019 was in fact rejected as not pressed on 30-6-2019 by a Bench of the High Court Division presided over by one of us (Syed Refaat Ahmed, J.) and that therefore the prior Writ Petition never came up for substantive consideration by this Court. The learned DAG's submissions in this context are found, accordingly, to be without merit and, therefore, not to our satisfaction. 

20. Mr Kamal-ul Alam has painstakingly explained the entire process of assessment and the initiation of that process through the delivery of the IGM in respect of the vessel, the mode and manner of its registration, electronic transmission and receipt, the procedural requirements for assessment, the evidentiary value of transmitted documents and indeed of the contents and details recorded therein to fully explain to this Court the substantive foundation and merit of the Petitioner's case before us. In that exercise of highlighting the relevant provisions of law dealing with clearance and assessment of taxes etc. the Petitioner's journey like any other importer in its situation begins for our purpose with section 43 of the Act as deals with delivery of IGM in respect of the relevant vessel on which the cargo enters the territorial waters of Bangladesh. The gist of section 43(1) and (2) is that any vessel arriving in Bangladesh shall enter through the place in any river or port fixed by the NBR through gazette notification and beyond which such vessel shall not pass until an IGM has been delivered to the relevant Customs Authority or other person duly authorised to receive the same, or as the case may be, until the manifest has been transmitted to the Customs computer system by a registered user. Concomitantly, by reference to section 79 of the Act the owner of the imported goods shall through a bill of entry delivered to an appropriate officer ensure that preliminary steps are taken for entry of imported goods for home consumption, warehousing or any other purposes into Bangladesh. Mr Kamal-ul Alam explains satisfactorily that once the IGM has either been physically filed or electronically transmitted the filing or transmission of a bill of entry necessary follows.

21. These conditionalities being fulfilled, the provisions of section 80 of the Act step in for the purpose of assessment of duty. Such assessment can only take place upon either the physical delivery or as in this case the electronic transmission of the relevant Bill of Entry. The assessment of duty further must follow and be founded upon the rate prevailing on the date that a Bill of Entry is delivered as provided under section 79 above referred. Accordingly, section 30 states simply and clearly: 
"30. Date for determination of rate of duty and tariff value of imported goods.—The rate of duty and tariff value, if any, applicable to any imported goods, shall be the rate of duty and tariff value in force on the date a bill of entry is delivered under section 79." 

22. It is the Petitioner's contention that the date in question as has been attracted to operate in the Petitioner's favour in the facts is 12-6-2019. It has not to be lost sight of that all these procedural niceties had played out in the facts against the backdrop of the requirements, conditionalities and procedural requirements set out in the notice dated 11-6-2019 as above reproduced. It is in this context that Mr Kamal-ul Alam has explained at length further the process of electronic transmission of Bill of entry under the law. 

23. Mr Alam by reference to section 79D of the Act highlights that only registered users of the Customs computer system can access and use the Customs transmission mechanism as referred to in certain provisions of the Act as already noted. Key to such access and use of the Customs computer system is the allocation and acquisition of a unique user identifier (UUI) for use in relation to the Customs computer system. Section 79D(2) categorically asserts that the UUI: "shall be used by the registered user for the purpose of transmitting information to or receiving information from that [customs computer] system" 

24. This Court is apprised by the parties in confirmation of the fact as noted at the very outset in this Judgment that the Customs computer system as envisaged in section 79D has been devised in this country as per UNCTAD specifications allowing for a universal and uniform advanced software regime commonly known as the Automated System for Customs Data or ASYCUDA. 

25. There are additionally other issues attendant to the use of the UUI that are of legal consequence and which have additionally been addressed extensively by the Act. It is here that Mr Kamal-ul Alam has taken care to explain that the law clothes the fact of transmission of information through the Customs computer i.e., the ASYCUDA World System with considerable evidentiary value in terms of who transmits such information and setting at the same time a high threshold for dislodging such value. Accordingly, section 79E(1) of the Act as deals expressly with the use of the UUI provides that: 
"79E. Use of unique user identifier-(1) Where information is transmitted to a [customs computer] system using a unique user identifier issued to a registered user by the Commissioner of Customs for that purpose, the transmission of that information shall, in the absence of proof to the contrary, be sufficient evidence that the registered user to whom the unique user identifier has been issued has transmitted that information." 

26. Furthermore, the data generated by such transmission of information by the holder of a UUI necessarily requires protection and security extended under the law. The law in the form of the Act, as Mr Kamal-ul Alam satisfactorily submits, amply extends that protection under section 79G. Accordingly, the Customs Authority significantly emerges as the keeper of records or data information generated by a importer as the Petitioner under section 79G which mandatorily requires that the Customs Authority "must keep a record of every transmission sent to or received from a registered user using a 'Customs computer] system". It is equally incumbent upon the Customs Authority under section 79G(2) to maintain such record or data for a period of five years from the date of transmission or receipt allowing also for the variation of such period as may be prescribed from time to time. It is here in section 79G that a Customs functionary like the Respondent No. 2, Commissioner is reminded by the law and now by this Court to discharge his onus in the facts of disproving the Petitioner's core contention that such transmission of all relevant information pertaining to the IGM and the Bill of Entry took place strictly in compliance with the provisions of the law as above explained and on the material date of 12-6-2019. This Court finds that the Respondent No. 2, Commissioner has, however, miserably failed to discharge that onus either by reference to the law and the documents on record or indeed the express provisions of the notice of 11-6-2019. 

27. This Court has at this juncture under-taken a thorough and detailed survey of the contents of the transmitted documents by the Petitioner's learned Advocate Mr Kamal-ul Alam only to be satisfied of the fact that the Petitioner had used its UUI registration number to obtain and secure at the initial phase an IGM Number as a necessary prelude to the aborted transmission of its Bill of Entry through the ASYCUDA World System up to a certain hour of 12-6-2019 but was repeatedly and irregularly thwarted by a systemic blockage from effectively doing so. It is also Mr Kamal-ul Alam's assertion to the satisfaction of this Court that all the information contained in the transmitted documents or recorded and generated though the ASYCUDA World System by a certain hour of 12-6-2019 would be evidence enough of relevant information and data generated under the law by using the Customs computer system that would entitle the Petitioner to avail fully of the benefit of assessment of duty prevailing at the rate as was current on 12-6-2019 from the very first attempt the Petitioner made at transmitting the Annexure-'E series' documents through to the Customs Authority. It follows further that the Court is also satisfied that the above facts being established the Petitioner remains well within the ambit of the beneficial operation of the notice of 11-6-2019 and especially clauses 1(ka) and (cha) and clause 2 of the said notice to claim the benefit of assessment under section 80 read with section 30 of the Act with the operative date being 12-6-2019. 

28. Significantly further, the Annexure- 'D' IGM generated through the ASYCUDA World System attests to this Court's satisfaction the fact that the concerned vessel MV Heilan Brother arrived on 12-6-2019 at 3-53 pm and that the said IGM clearly bears UUI No. 2019 in satisfaction of the requirements of section 79 of the Act as well as IGM No. 2104. As earlier noted, the Respondent No. 2, Commissioner has speciously submitted that absent a countersignature by the relevant Customs Authority the IGM as transmitted is of no legal consequence. But in accepting Mr Kamal-ul Alam's rebuttal as already above noted, this Court finds to the contrary that section 46 understandably and necessarily does away with the requirement of an actual counter-signature in favour of a presumption of such a countersignature when the import manifest is transmitted electronically as in this case to the concerned Customs Officer through the Customs computer system ASYCUDA by a registered user such as the Petitioner using his UUI No. 2019. 

29. Indeed, contrary to what both the Respondent No. 2, Commissioner asserts and has been submitted by the learned DAG on reliance of the same, this Court finds that in the circumstances it was absolutely and unconditionally incumbent upon the relevant Customs Authority or Officer to accept the transmitted 1GM at its face value. This, it is found, the Respondents in the facts clearly are reluctant so to do without the aid of any legal provision that supports their position. Having gone through the Annexure-'E series' documents with a fine-tooth comb, this Court finds clear evidence of three attempts at transmitting Bill of Entry No. 301 at 4-04 pm, 4-11 pm and 4-16 pm in quick succession with a sense of desperation evident in that sheer effort by the Petitioner to stay well within the parameters of the assessment process so declared ostensibly in the public interest through the notice of 11-6-2019. Every such single attempt is equally found by this Court to have been ominously thwarted by an information bar in red imprinted on the ASYCUDA generated document reading "stop-error: budget update: b/e registration will resume by June, 13, 05-00 pm". Accordingly, it is our finding, and for want of a better and more plausible explanation to the contrary offered by the Respondents, that the Petitioner was unreasonably and unfairly stopped at the gates of due and proper assessment on 12-6-2019 as indeed was its entitlement under the law, and that too a day earlier then declared in the notice of 11-6-2019, without further explanation and assumption of due responsibility for such systemic error and contingency by the concerned Respondents. This single error has had the effect of negating the substantive operation of all provisions of the Act as above quoted and indeed the notice of 11-6-2019 in a manner that boggles the mind leading this Court to find that no reasonable authority as the Customs Authority would have let this matter go unchecked without extending any relief to the Petitioner or somebody in its position faced with this predicament. Therein lies the crux of the Petitioner's case as to why the Petitioner should inexplicably, unreasonably and unwarrantedly be penalized for a systemic breakdown of the Customs' own automated mechanism for assessment. This Court notes at no time in these proceedings has any of the Respondents assumed any responsibility for such glaring systemic failure but have individually and collectively instead sought to burden the Petitioner in all manners and with all devices to explain its case when it is otherwise wholly the Respondents' responsibility to do so with utmost care. 

30. The notice of 11-6-2019 itself makes clear that all vessels arriving between 11-6-2019 and 13-6-2019 would have the privilege secured unconditionally of 1GM transmission and that the transmission mechanism will be closed on the Budget date with regard to Bills of Entry between 11-00 pm 13-6-2019 to 9-00 pm 14-6-2019. However, under cover of this systemic error the Respondents appear to this Court deliberately to have taken liberty, for reasons this Court can at best speculate on, with both the applicable standards of law and the requirements of the notice in a manner most irregular and reprehensible to defeat the vested interests and rights of an importer as the Petitioner. 

31. On an additional question of the maintainability of this Writ Petition and in yet another blatant attempt at saddling an importer like the Petitioner with undue responsibility to establish its case which otherwise is clearly governed and supported by the law to the benefit of the Petitioner, the Respondent No. 2 Commissioner, and as represented by the learned DAG, has attempted and argued that judicial review is not an appropriate forum for the Petitioner to seek redress in the given facts given that to the Commissioner's under-standing this case deals with disputed questions of facts. In this regard, the Commissioner points to the avenue available for a ruling under section 219A of the Act. This Court can only hasten to alert the Respondent No. 2, Commissioner to the fact that the exercise above undertaken by this Court at the Petitioner's behest to highlight, analyse and apply the law to the Petitioner's benefit as above is alone indicative of the fact that the Petitioner's case is governed purely by law and not shorn of law as the Respondent No. 2, Commissioner would have this Court find otherwise. Accordingly, this case has all the ingredients to merit a judicial review of the actions of the Customs authority as has indeed been accomplished above. 

32. We note further that there is a reference made by the Respondent No. 2, Commissioner to the Provisional Collection of Taxes Act, 1931, albeit in the passing and without further elaboration, in the Affidavit-in-Opposition. The learned DAG has aptly submitted, however, that the 1931 Act has no manner of application in the present facts and that it is not attracted in the circumstances for this Court's consideration at all. In this regard, the Respondent No. 2 Commissioner's attention is drawn to this very Court's judgment in Writ Petition No. 6713 of 2019 on the application of the Provisional Collection of Taxes Act, 1931. We deem it unnecessary to embark upon an exercise involving the 1931 Act at the present time given our understanding that it has no manner of application to the present case. 

33. In conclusion, this Court finds the purported action of the Respondent No. 2, Commissioner in shutting down the ASYCUDA World System on 12-6-2019 form 3-53 pm onwards to be in blatant violation of the notice dated 11-6-2019 and, thereby, finds further the prevention of the due registration of the Petitioner's Bill of Entry on 12-6-2019 to be unlawful, illegal, without lawful authority and to be of no legal effect. Consequentially, the Respondent No. 2 is, hereby, directed to ensure the registration of the Petitioner's Bill of Entry in full compliance with the notice dated 11-6-2019 and levy Customs duty on the Petitioner's consignment at the rate as prevailing on 12-6-2019 within a period of 3 (three) weeks from the date of receipt of the certified copy of this Judgment and Order. 

34. In light of the above, this Court having found merit in the Application and substance in the Rule issued, resultantly, makes this Rule absolute. 

35. There is no Order as to costs. 

Communicate this judgment and order along with the judgment in Writ Petition No. 6713 of 2019 at once. 

End.

full_judgment:
Md. Nazrul Islam Talukder, J:
1. On an application under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People’s Republic of Bangladesh, the Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned notices dated 19.03.2019 under MemoNo.00.01.0000.502.01. 007. 19/10746 and Memo No.00.01.0000.502.01. 007. 19/10745 respectively under Sections 19 and 20 of the Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004 and Rule 20 of the Anti-Corruption Commission Rules, 2007 read with Section 160 of the Code of Criminal Procedure issued by the Respondent No.3 (Annexure-Q and Q-1) directing the petitioners to appear and make statement regarding evasion of registration fees and taxes at the time of purchase and registration of the land in question, before the Respondent No.3 following the application dated 11.12.2018 (Annexure-N) filed by the Respondent No.5, shall not be declared to have been passed/issued without lawful authority and are of no legal effect and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.
2. The facts leading to issuance of the Rule Nisi are as follows:
(a) that Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sangstha (in short BSRS), now Bangladesh Development Bank Limited (in short BDBL) filed Miscellaneous Case No.15 of 1987 before the Court of learned District Judge, Dhaka under the provision of President Order No.128 of 1972 against the Respondent No.5’s Company namely the United Trading Corporation Limited for realization of its loan. By an order dated 25.08.1989, the learned trial Judge attached the schedule property before the judgment. Thereafter the said Miscellaneous Case No.15 of 1987 was transferred to the Court of learned Subordinate Judge and the Artha Rin Adalat, Dhaka, 2nd Court and the same was renumbered as Title Suit No. 01 of 1999. The suit was decreed on 24.05.1999 in favour of the successor of BSRS i.e. Bangladesh Development Bank Limited (hereinafter referred to as BDBL). The aforesaid fact is evident from the judgment and decree dated 24.05.1999 passed in Title Suit No.1 of 1999 which are annexed with the writ petition and marked as Annexure-A and A-1.

(b) that on 31.05.1999, BDBL filed Artha Execution Case No.18 of 1999 for an amount of Tk.3,62,83,864.84/- (three crore sixty two lac eighty three thousand eight hundred sixty four taka eighty four paisa) only and the attached scheduled land was sold at a price of Tk. 25 crore to the petitioners namely Standard Stitches Limited and Standard Group Limited and one Md. Arifur Rahman and the Respondent No.4 under Section 38 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 and accordingly, the execution Court executed a registered sale certificate dated 27.02.2013 in favour of the purchasers and delivered possession of the suit land to the purchasers on 20.05.2014 pursuant to the Sale Certificate No. 5 dated 27.02.2013 through writ for delivery of possession. 24. We have gone through the writ petition, the supplementary affidavits and the affidavit- in-oppositions submitted by the Respondent Nos.2 and 5 and perused all the materials annexed therewith.
